title: On Nature (fragments)
creator: heraclitus
location: Ephesus; deposited, by tradition, in the Temple of Artemis
note: About a hundred riddling sayings on flux, the Logos and the unity of opposites.
description: Heraclitus wrote a single book, which ancient tradition says he deposited in the great Temple of Artemis at Ephesus. It is lost, and what survives are around a hundred short sayings quoted, often for their own purposes, by authors from Plato and Aristotle to the Christian bishop Hippolytus and the sceptic Sextus Empiricus. The fragments are compressed, paradoxical and deliberately difficult: the Logos is common to all yet most people do not understand it; the way up and the way down are one and the same; war is the father of all; the cosmos is an ever-living fire kindled and extinguished in measures. Their original order is unknown, and modern editions, especially the numbering of Diels and Kranz, are reconstructions. Read alongside Parmenides, they frame the central problem of Presocratic thought, and they have fascinated readers from the Stoics to Hegel, Nietzsche and Heidegger.

title: On Nature (poem)
creator: parmenides
location: Elea, southern Italy
note: A goddess reveals the Way of Truth: what is cannot come to be, change or be divided.
description: Parmenides set out his philosophy in epic hexameter verse, in the manner of Homer and Hesiod, with a proem in which a young man rides a chariot through the gates of Night and Day to meet a goddess. She teaches him two ways: the Way of Truth, which concerns only 'what is', and the Way of Opinion, a cosmology of mortal belief. About 160 lines survive, most of them preserved by the sixth-century commentator Simplicius, who copied out long passages because the book was already rare. The central argument is a chain of deductions: since what is not cannot be thought or spoken of, what is must be ungenerated, imperishable, whole, unmoving and complete. This is often called the first sustained argument in Western philosophy, and it set the agenda for Zeno, Empedocles, the atomists and Plato's Parmenides and Sophist.
image_caption: On Nature (poem): early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Apology
creator: socrates
location: Athens
note: Plato's version of Socrates' defence speech at his trial for impiety and corrupting the young.
description: The Apology, written by Plato within a few years of the trial of 399 BC, presents the speech Socrates gave in his own defence before a jury of 501 Athenian citizens. 'Apology' here means defence, not apology. Socrates explains that the Delphic oracle declared no one wiser than he, and that by questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen he found that he alone knew that he did not know. He cross-examines his accuser Meletus, refuses to stop philosophising even to save his life, and, after the guilty verdict, provocatively proposes as his 'penalty' free meals at public expense. It contains the claims that the unexamined life is not worth living and that no harm can come to a good man. How closely it records what Socrates actually said is debated; Xenophon also wrote an Apology with a different emphasis. It is the usual starting point for reading Plato and for meeting Socrates.

title: Republic
creator: plato
location: Athens (the Academy)
note: What is justice, and is the just person happier? The answer builds an ideal city, the Forms and the Cave.
description: The Republic, in ten books, is Plato's most famous dialogue. It opens with Socrates and friends at the Piraeus asking what justice is; Thrasymachus argues that justice is the advantage of the stronger, and Glaucon and Adeimantus challenge Socrates to show that justice is worth having for its own sake. To find justice in the soul, Socrates constructs an ideal city with three classes, producers, auxiliaries and philosopher-guardians, and argues that a soul is just when reason rules spirit and appetite. The middle books introduce the philosopher-kings, the Form of the Good compared to the sun, the Divided Line and the allegory of the Cave. Later books describe the decline of constitutions into tyranny, banish most poetry from the city, and close with the Myth of Er about the soul's fate after death. The Republic founded political philosophy and has been admired, attacked (most famously by Karl Popper) and endlessly reinterpreted.
image_caption: Opening of the Republic in a 9th-century Byzantine manuscript (Codex Parisinus graecus 1807)

title: Phaedo
creator: plato
location: Athens (the Academy)
note: Socrates' last day: arguments for the soul's immortality and the theory of Forms.
description: The Phaedo is narrated by Phaedo of Elis, who was present on the day Socrates drank the hemlock. In the prison, Socrates argues to his Pythagorean-influenced friends Simmias and Cebes that the true philosopher does not fear death, since philosophy is practice for dying, the separation of soul from body. He offers a series of arguments for the soul's immortality: from opposites, from recollection, from the soul's affinity with the unchanging Forms, and finally from the Form of Life itself. Along the way he tells of his youthful disappointment with Anaxagoras' natural science. The dialogue ends with a myth of the earth and the moving scene of Socrates' death. It is one of the main sources for Plato's theory of Forms, and its picture of the soul shaped Christian ideas of immortality.
image_caption: Phaedo: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Symposium
creator: plato
location: Athens (the Academy)
note: Speeches in praise of love at a drinking party, ending with Diotima's ladder of beauty.
description: The Symposium is set at a drinking party in 416 BC celebrating the tragedian Agathon's victory. The guests agree to give speeches in praise of Eros, the god of love. Aristophanes tells the comic myth that humans were once double creatures split in two, and love is the longing for our other half. Socrates recounts what the priestess Diotima taught him: love is desire for the good to be one's own for ever, and the lover should ascend from love of one beautiful body to all bodies, to souls, laws and knowledge, and finally to Beauty itself. The drunken Alcibiades then bursts in and gives a portrait of Socrates' strange self-control. The dialogue is a literary masterpiece and the source of the idea of 'Platonic love'.
image_caption: Fragment of the Symposium on papyrus from Oxyrhynchus

title: Timaeus
creator: plato
location: Athens (the Academy)
note: A cosmology: a divine craftsman shapes the world after eternal models out of geometrical elements.
description: In the Timaeus, the astronomer Timaeus of Locri gives a 'likely account' of the origin of the cosmos. A divine craftsman, the Demiurge, looking to an eternal model, imposes order on a disorderly receptacle, making the world a living being with a soul; the four elements are built from triangles forming regular solids. The dialogue also tells the story of Atlantis. Its relation to Plato's other works and whether the creation story is meant literally were debated already in antiquity. For centuries much of it was the only Plato available in Latin, in Calcidius' partial translation, and it dominated medieval cosmology; Raphael's School of Athens shows Plato holding it.
image_caption: Opening of the Timaeus in a 9th-century Byzantine manuscript (Codex Parisinus graecus 1807)

title: Nicomachean Ethics
creator: aristotle
location: Athens (the Lyceum)
note: Happiness as activity in accordance with virtue; virtue as a mean; practical wisdom and friendship.
description: The Nicomachean Ethics, in ten books, probably takes its name from Aristotle's son Nicomachus, who may have edited it. It asks what the highest human good is and answers eudaimonia, happiness or flourishing, understood as a complete life of activity of the soul in accordance with virtue. Moral virtues are stable dispositions, formed by habit, to feel and act rightly, lying in a mean between excess and deficiency relative to us, as courage lies between rashness and cowardice; the right mean is fixed by practical wisdom (phronēsis). The work also discusses voluntary action, justice, weakness of will, pleasure and, at length, friendship, and ends by praising the contemplative life as the highest happiness. It was the basis of ethics in medieval universities and is the main text of modern virtue ethics.
image_caption: Nicomachean Ethics: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Metaphysics
creator: aristotle
location: Athens (the Lyceum)
note: The science of being as being: substance, form and matter, potentiality and actuality, the unmoved mover.
description: The Metaphysics is a collection of fourteen books on what Aristotle called first philosophy or wisdom; the title, meaning 'after the Physics', was probably given by an ancient editor. It opens with the claim that all humans by nature desire to know, reviews earlier thinkers' views of first causes, and defends the principle of non-contradiction. Its central books ask what substance is, and answer in terms of form, essence and the compound of form and matter; others analyse potentiality and actuality. Book Lambda argues for an eternal unmoved mover, pure actuality, thought thinking itself, which moves the heavens as an object of love. Transmitted through Arabic and Latin commentaries, it shaped Avicenna, Averroes, Aquinas and the whole medieval tradition.
image_caption: Page from a medieval manuscript of the Metaphysics in William of Moerbeke's Latin translation

title: Politics
creator: aristotle
location: Athens (the Lyceum)
note: Humans as political animals; the household and slavery; classification and comparison of constitutions.
description: Aristotle's Politics, in eight books, argues that the city (polis) exists by nature and that a human being is a political animal, since only in a city can we live well. It discusses the household, including a notorious defence of 'natural' slavery and of male rule, criticises Plato's Republic, classifies constitutions by whether one, few or many rule and whether they rule for the common good, and recommends a mixed 'polity' based on a large middle class. Its later books describe an ideal city and its education. The work drew on studies of 158 Greek constitutions made in the Lyceum. Translated into Latin in the thirteenth century, it shaped medieval and early modern political thought.

title: Poetics
creator: aristotle
location: Athens (the Lyceum)
note: Tragedy as imitation of an action, with plot, reversal, recognition and catharsis.
description: The Poetics is the earliest surviving work of literary theory. Aristotle treats poetry as mimēsis, imitation, natural to humans, and analyses tragedy as the imitation of a serious, complete action that through pity and fear accomplishes the catharsis of such emotions. Plot is the soul of tragedy, and the best plots turn on reversal and recognition caused by a hero's error (hamartia); Sophocles' Oedipus the King is his model. A second book on comedy is lost. Rediscovered in the Renaissance, the Poetics shaped neoclassical drama and its 'unities', and remains a reference point for theories of narrative.

title: Letter to Menoeceus
creator: epicurus
location: Athens (the Garden)
note: A compact summary of Epicurean ethics: do not fear the gods or death; pleasure is freedom from pain.
description: The Letter to Menoeceus is one of three letters by Epicurus preserved by Diogenes Laertius in his Lives of the Eminent Philosophers. In a few pages it sets out the core of Epicurean ethics for a general reader. The gods are blessed and immortal and do not concern themselves with us. Death is nothing to us, since when we are, death is not, and when death is, we are not. Desires are natural and necessary, natural but unnecessary, or empty, and the wise satisfy the first simply. Pleasure is the beginning and end of the blessed life, but not the pleasures of the profligate: rather the absence of pain in the body and of trouble in the soul, reached by sober reasoning. It is the best short introduction to Epicurus.

title: Outlines of Pyrrhonism
creator: skeptics
location: Probably Alexandria or Rome (uncertain)
note: Sextus Empiricus' handbook of Pyrrhonian scepticism: opposing arguments, suspension of judgment, tranquillity.
description: The Outlines of Pyrrhonism by the physician Sextus Empiricus, written around the late second century AD, is the fullest surviving account of ancient scepticism. Book I explains the sceptical 'way': setting appearances and arguments against one another until their equal force leads to suspension of judgment, followed by tranquillity, and sets out the Ten Modes of Aenesidemus and the Five Modes of Agrippa, standard patterns for generating doubt. Books II and III apply the method to logic, physics and ethics. Latin translations printed in 1562 and 1569 had a dramatic effect on European thought, feeding the scepticism of Montaigne and the arguments of Descartes, Bayle and Hume.

title: Moral Letters to Lucilius
creator: seneca
location: Rome and Campania
note: Practical Stoicism in letters to a friend: time, friendship, death, wealth and daily self-examination.
description: In his last years, after withdrawing from Nero's court, Seneca wrote 124 letters to his younger friend Lucilius, then procurator of Sicily. Whether they were actually sent or written for publication is debated. Each letter starts from an everyday occasion, a visit to a villa, a sea voyage, the noise of a bath-house, and draws a lesson: that time is our only possession, that the wise person needs nothing yet values friends, that death is to be rehearsed, that philosophy shapes the soul rather than amusing the mind. Seneca often quotes Epicurus approvingly. The letters were read by Christians in the Middle Ages, by Montaigne, Bacon and the Renaissance essayists, and have become a bestseller of the modern Stoic revival.
image_file: Seneca the Younger, Letters, Florence, Plut. 45.33.jpg
image_caption: Medieval manuscript of Seneca's Letters, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence (Plut. 45.33)

title: Enchiridion (Handbook)
creator: epictetus
location: Nicopolis, Epirus
note: The dichotomy of control in fifty-three short chapters: some things are up to us, others are not.
description: The Enchiridion, meaning 'handbook' or 'thing ready to hand', is a short digest of Epictetus' teaching made by his pupil Arrian, who also recorded the longer Discourses. It opens with the famous distinction between what is up to us, our opinions, impulses, desires and aversions, and what is not, our body, property, reputation and office. Disturbance comes not from things but from our judgments about them, so we should train ourselves to want things to happen as they do happen. It was adapted for use by Christian monks, printed with a Latin translation by Angelo Poliziano in the fifteenth century, and widely read in the early modern period; it is now a standard introduction to Stoic practice and a forerunner of cognitive therapy.
image_caption: Enchiridion (Handbook): early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Meditations
creator: marcus-aurelius
location: On campaign on the Danube frontier, and Rome
note: An emperor's private Stoic exercises: impermanence, duty and acceptance of nature's order.
description: The Meditations are twelve books of notes that Marcus Aurelius wrote in Greek for himself, probably during his last decade and partly on campaign against Germanic tribes; the first book records what he learned from family and teachers, and one is headed 'among the Quadi'. They were not meant for publication, and the title is modern; the Greek manuscripts call them 'to himself'. Marcus reminds himself to accept what happens as part of a rational whole, to treat others as kin even when they are difficult, to do his duty without complaint, and to keep in view the brevity of life and the vastness of time. The first printed edition appeared in Zurich in 1558. They became one of the most widely read works of ancient philosophy.
image_file: Marcus Aurelius. De seipso, seu vita sua (Xylander, 1558).jpg
image_caption: Title page of the first printed edition, edited by Wilhelm Xylander, Zurich, 1558

title: Enneads
creator: plotinus
location: Rome
note: The One, Intellect and Soul, and the soul's ascent to union with its source.
description: Plotinus wrote fifty-four treatises in the last seventeen years of his life, in response to questions raised in his seminars in Rome. His pupil Porphyry edited them around 301 into six groups of nine, the Enneads (from the Greek for 'nine'), ordered roughly from ethics and the world to soul, intellect and the One, and prefaced them with a life of his teacher. The treatises are dense and exploratory, arguing with Aristotle, the Stoics and the Gnostics. They describe reality as unfolding from the One through Intellect and Soul, and the soul's path back through virtue, beauty and contemplation. Marsilio Ficino's Latin translation of 1492 brought Plotinus to the Renaissance.

title: Confessions
creator: augustine
location: Hippo Regius, North Africa
note: Augustine's story of his restless heart, from childhood theft to conversion, followed by reflections on memory, time and creation.
description: The Confessions, written soon after Augustine became bishop of Hippo, are addressed throughout to God. Books I to IX tell his life: an infancy already marked by sin, the theft of pears for the pleasure of wrongdoing, his student years in Carthage, his attraction to Manichaeism, his career as a rhetorician, his long relationship with an unnamed woman, the influence of Ambrose and Neoplatonist books, and the conversion in a Milan garden where he heard a child's voice say 'take up and read'. Book IX ends with the death of his mother Monica. Books X to XIII turn to memory, the nature of time and the creation story of Genesis. Often called the first Western autobiography, it profoundly shaped later writing about the self, from Petrarch to Rousseau.
image_caption: Confessions: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: The City of God
creator: augustine
location: Hippo Regius, North Africa
note: After the sack of Rome: the earthly city of self-love and the heavenly city of love of God.
description: The City of God was begun after Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, when pagans blamed the disaster on the abandonment of the old gods. In the first ten books Augustine argues that the gods never protected Rome and that pagan philosophy, even Platonism, cannot bring happiness. The remaining twelve books trace the origin, history and destinies of two cities: the earthly city, founded on love of self to the contempt of God, and the heavenly city, founded on love of God to the contempt of self. They are intermingled in history and separated only at the Last Judgment. The work offers a theology of history, discussions of war, peace and the state, and a reading of Roman history. It shaped medieval political thought and Christian ideas of history.
image_caption: Manuscript of The City of God

title: The Consolation of Philosophy
creator: boethius
type: Dialogue in prose and verse (5 books)
location: Prison near Pavia
note: Awaiting execution, Boethius is consoled by Lady Philosophy: fortune, true happiness, providence and free will.
description: Boethius wrote the Consolation while imprisoned awaiting execution on charges of treason against King Theodoric. In alternating prose and verse, it begins with the author lamenting his fate, until Philosophy appears as a majestic woman and drives away the Muses of poetry. She diagnoses his sickness as forgetfulness of his true nature, shows that Fortune's gifts are not true goods, argues that true happiness is God, explains why the wicked seem to prosper, and finally reconciles divine foreknowledge with human freedom by arguing that God sees all time in an eternal present. It draws on Plato, Aristotle and the Neoplatonists and does not mention Christ. It was one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages, translated by King Alfred, Chaucer and Elizabeth I.
image_caption: The Consolation of Philosophy: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Periphyseon (On the Division of Nature)
creator: eriugena
location: Court of Charles the Bald, Francia
note: Nature divided into four: what creates and is not created, through to what neither creates nor is created.
description: The Periphyseon is a long dialogue between a teacher and a pupil. Eriugena divides 'nature', meaning everything that is and is not, into four: what creates and is not created, God as source; what is created and creates, the primordial causes; what is created and does not create, the world of things in space and time; and what neither creates nor is created, God as the goal to which all things return. Drawing on Pseudo-Dionysius, Gregory of Nyssa and Maximus the Confessor, whom he translated, he develops a negative theology in which God transcends all categories. It is the most ambitious philosophical system of the early Middle Ages. Its suspected pantheism led to its condemnation by Pope Honorius III in 1225.
image_caption: Manuscript of the Periphyseon from Reims, c. 875

title: The Book of Healing (al-Shifa)
creator: avicenna
location: Hamadan and Isfahan, Persia
note: Avicenna's great system of logic, natural science, mathematics and metaphysics, built on Aristotle.
description: The Book of Healing, meaning the healing of the soul from ignorance, is Avicenna's philosophical encyclopaedia. It covers logic, natural philosophy (including psychology), mathematics and metaphysics, reworking Aristotle with ideas of his own and of the Neoplatonists. It contains the distinction between essence and existence, the proof of God as the Necessary Existent, an account of emanation through a series of intellects, and in the psychology the 'Flying Man' argument for the soul's self-awareness. Parts of it were translated into Latin in Toledo in the twelfth century, where they deeply influenced Albert the Great, Aquinas and Duns Scotus.

title: Canon of Medicine
creator: avicenna
location: Hamadan, Persia
note: The standard medical textbook of the Islamic world and medieval Europe for centuries.
description: Avicenna's Canon of Medicine systematised the medicine of Galen and Hippocrates with Aristotelian natural philosophy and his own clinical observations. Its five books cover general principles, medicinal substances, diseases of particular organs, diseases affecting the whole body, and compound drugs. It discusses contagion, quarantine and the testing of drugs. Translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona in the twelfth century, it became a standard textbook in European universities into the seventeenth century, and illuminated manuscripts and early printed editions survive in large numbers. It shows Avicenna's conviction that medicine is a science grounded in philosophy.
image_caption: Canon of Medicine: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Proslogion
creator: anselm
location: Abbey of Bec, Normandy
note: The ontological argument: God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived.
description: Anselm wrote the Proslogion, meaning 'address', as a prayerful meditation in search of a single argument for God's existence; he said the idea came to him after long struggle. Chapter 2 argues that even the fool who says in his heart there is no God understands the phrase 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived'; since existing in reality is greater than existing only in the understanding, such a being must exist in reality. Chapter 3 argues that it cannot even be conceived not to exist. The monk Gaunilo replied with the example of a perfect island, and Anselm's response was copied with the work. The argument was rejected by Aquinas, revived by Descartes and Leibniz, criticised by Kant and reformulated in modal logic in the twentieth century.
image_caption: Illuminated initial from a manuscript of Anselm's Monologion

title: Scivias
creator: hildegard
location: Disibodenberg and Rupertsberg, Rhineland
note: Twenty-six visions of creation, redemption and the church, with striking illuminations.
description: Scivias, from the Latin for 'know the ways', records twenty-six visions that Hildegard experienced and explained over ten years, with the help of her secretary, the monk Volmar. She describes each vision and then gives its interpretation in the voice of God. The three books treat creation and the fall, redemption through Christ and the church, and the history of salvation to the end of time, closing with songs. The famous Rupertsberg manuscript, made under her supervision around 1165–80, had thirty-five remarkable illuminations; it was lost in the Second World War, but a hand-painted facsimile made by nuns of Eibingen in the 1920s survives. Pope Eugenius III read part of it at the Synod of Trier in 1147–48 and encouraged her to continue.
image_caption: Illumination from the Scivias (Rupertsberg codex tradition)

title: Decisive Treatise
creator: averroes
location: Seville or Córdoba, al-Andalus
note: Islamic law commands philosophy for those able, and demonstrative truth cannot conflict with scripture.
description: In the Decisive Treatise, written as a legal opinion (fatwa), Averroes asks whether the study of philosophy is permitted, forbidden or commanded by Islamic law. He argues that the Qur'an commands reflection on creation, that demonstration is the highest form of reflection, and that philosophy is therefore obligatory for those capable of it. People differ in their capacity: some are persuaded by rhetoric, some by dialectic, a few by demonstration. Since truth does not contradict truth, where scripture's apparent meaning conflicts with demonstration it must be interpreted allegorically, but such interpretations should not be revealed to the masses. The treatise was little known in the Latin West but is now central to discussions of faith and reason in Islam.

title: The Guide for the Perplexed
creator: maimonides
location: Fustat (Old Cairo), Egypt
note: For a student torn between Torah and philosophy: figurative reading of scripture and negative theology.
description: The Guide for the Perplexed, written in Arabic in Hebrew letters as a letter to a student, Joseph ben Judah, addresses readers who are troubled by apparent conflicts between the literal meaning of scripture and philosophy. The first part explains biblical terms for God as figurative and develops a negative theology: God has no positive attributes, and we approach knowledge of God by understanding what God is not. The second discusses proofs of God's existence and the question of whether the world was created or eternal, which Maimonides held cannot be demonstrated either way. The third treats prophecy, providence, evil and the reasons for the commandments. It was translated into Hebrew in his lifetime and into Latin by the 1240s, provoked bitter controversy among Jews, and influenced Aquinas and Spinoza.

image_caption: Manuscript page of the Guide in Arabic in Hebrew letters

title: Summa Theologiae
creator: aquinas
location: Rome, Paris and Naples
note: The grandest scholastic synthesis: God, creation, human nature, ethics, law and Christ, in disputed questions.
description: Aquinas wrote the Summa Theologiae as a guide for beginners in theology, though it runs to some three thousand articles. Each article poses a question, gives objections, cites an authority 'on the contrary', presents Aquinas' answer and replies to each objection. The First Part treats God, including the Five Ways of proving God's existence, creation, angels and human nature; the Second Part treats ethics, happiness, the passions, virtues and law, including the treatise on natural law; the Third Part treats Christ and the sacraments. He stopped writing in December 1273 and it was completed from his earlier work by his assistants. It became the central text of Catholic theology and, after Pope Leo XIII's encyclical of 1879, of the Thomist revival.
image_caption: Summa Theologiae: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Summa of Logic
creator: ockham
location: Oxford or London
note: Terms, propositions and arguments analysed with a nominalist theory of signification and supposition.
description: Ockham's Summa Logicae is one of the most important logic textbooks of the Middle Ages. The first part treats terms, the second propositions, and the third arguments, including syllogisms, demonstrations and fallacies. Its theory of signification and supposition explains how terms stand for things in propositions, and it develops a theory of mental language, a language of thought common to all humans, of which spoken and written languages are conventional signs. Throughout, Ockham uses logic to support nominalism: only individual things exist, and universals are signs that signify many individuals. It shaped the 'modern way' in late medieval universities.

title: On Learned Ignorance
creator: nicholas-of-cusa
location: Kues, Germany
note: Knowing that we cannot know the infinite precisely is the beginning of wisdom; in God opposites coincide.
description: Nicholas of Cusa said the idea for De docta ignorantia came to him on the sea voyage back from Constantinople in 1437–38. Book I argues that the finite mind can never grasp the infinite exactly, just as a polygon with ever more sides approaches but never becomes a circle; recognising this ignorance is learned. God is the absolute maximum, in whom maximum and minimum and all other opposites coincide, and Cusanus uses mathematical images, such as an infinite line being also a circle and a triangle, to point toward this. Book II argues that the universe has no fixed centre or circumference, so the earth cannot be the motionless centre. Book III treats Christ as the union of the maximum with the finite.

title: The Prince
creator: machiavelli
location: Written at Sant'Andrea in Percussina near Florence; printed in Rome and Florence, 1532
note: How a new prince gains and keeps power: virtù against fortuna, and acting against morality when necessary.
description: Machiavelli wrote The Prince in 1513, soon after being dismissed, imprisoned and tortured by the returning Medici, and dedicated it to Lorenzo de' Medici, apparently hoping for employment. It was circulated in manuscript and printed only in 1532, after his death. In twenty-six short chapters it surveys kinds of principalities, the use of arms, and the qualities a prince needs: it is better to be feared than loved if one cannot be both, a prince must know how to be a fox and a lion, and he must be ready not to be good when necessity requires. Cesare Borgia appears as a model of daring. The final chapter calls for a redeemer to free Italy from foreign invaders. The book was placed on the Index in 1559 and made Machiavelli's name a byword for cunning, but whether it is a manual for tyrants, a satire or a realistic analysis is still debated.

image_caption: Title page of an early edition of The Prince

title: Discourses on Livy
creator: machiavelli
location: Florence; printed in Rome and Florence, 1531
note: Why republics with armed citizens and open conflict between nobles and people last longest.
description: The Discourses on the First Ten Books of Titus Livy, written around 1513–19 for the discussion circle in the Orti Oricellari gardens in Florence, use the history of the Roman republic to draw lessons for modern politics. Machiavelli argues that Rome became free and great because of its mixed constitution and the conflict between patricians and plebeians, which produced laws favourable to liberty. Republics with citizen armies and periodic return to first principles are more durable and more capable of greatness than principalities, and the people are wiser and more constant than a prince. The book is the main source for Machiavelli the republican, and it influenced Harrington, the American founders and modern theories of republicanism.
image_file: Discorsi di Nicolo Machiavelli, firentino, sopra la prima deca di Tito Livio.jpg
image_caption: Discourses on Livy: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Essays
creator: montaigne
location: Château de Montaigne; first printed in Bordeaux, 1580
note: Attempts at self-knowledge on every topic, from cannibals and cruelty to friendship, experience and death.
description: Montaigne began writing his Essais, 'attempts' or 'trials', after retiring to his tower library in 1571. The first edition of 1580, printed in Bordeaux, had two books; a third was added in the Paris edition of 1588, and he kept writing additions in the margins of his copy, the 'Bordeaux copy', until his death. The posthumous edition of 1595 was prepared by Marie de Gournay. The essays range from short commentaries on classical examples to long, digressive explorations: 'Of Cannibals' contrasts Brazilian peoples with European cruelty, 'Of Friendship' commemorates La Boétie, the 'Apology for Raymond Sebond' develops Pyrrhonian scepticism, and 'Of Experience' ends in praise of an ordinary, embodied life. John Florio's English translation of 1603 was read by Shakespeare. The book created the essay as a genre.
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of Essays

title: Novum Organum
creator: francis-bacon
location: London
note: The idols of the mind and a new method of induction to replace Aristotle's logic.
description: The Novum Organum, or 'new instrument', was published in 1620 as part of Bacon's planned Instauratio Magna, a great renewal of the sciences; its title challenges Aristotle's logical works, known as the Organon. Its famous engraved title page shows a ship sailing between the Pillars of Hercules into the open ocean, with the motto that many will pass through and knowledge will be increased. Book I, in aphorisms, attacks existing learning and identifies the four idols that beset the mind: of the tribe (common to human nature), of the cave (individual), of the marketplace (from language) and of the theatre (from philosophical systems). Book II illustrates a new method of induction through tables of presence, absence and degree, applied to the nature of heat. It became a charter for the experimental science of the Royal Society.
image_caption: Novum Organum: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: New Atlantis
creator: francis-bacon
location: London (published with Sylva Sylvarum)
note: A utopian island ruled by Salomon's House, a state research institution devoted to the knowledge of causes.
description: New Atlantis is an unfinished utopian fable published in 1627, the year after Bacon's death, by his secretary William Rawley. European sailors lost in the Pacific land on the island of Bensalem, a Christian society of great order and courtesy. Its most important institution is Salomon's House, a college of scientists who conduct experiments in deep caves and high towers, run laboratories for medicine, optics, sound and engines, and send agents abroad to gather knowledge, all for 'the enlarging of the bounds of human empire'. The text breaks off before the planned account of the island's laws. It inspired the founders of the Royal Society and remains a touchstone for discussions of organised science.
image_file: Bacon 1628 New Atlantis title page wpreview.png
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of New Atlantis

title: Leviathan
creator: hobbes
location: Written in Paris; printed in London by Andrew Crooke, 1651
note: Without a sovereign, life is a war of all against all; people covenant to obey an absolute ruler.
description: Hobbes wrote Leviathan in exile in Paris during the English Civil War and published it in London in 1651. Its frontispiece, engraved by Abraham Bosse, shows a crowned giant made of hundreds of small human figures rising over a landscape, holding a sword and a crozier. Part I builds a materialist account of human nature from sensation, imagination and the passions, and argues that in a state of nature equal individuals would be at war, with life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'. Laws of nature, discovered by reason, direct them to seek peace by covenanting to authorise a sovereign. Part II argues that sovereign power must be undivided and absolute; Parts III and IV subordinate the church to the state and attack priestly authority. It was condemned as atheistic, but it founded modern political philosophy and social contract theory.
image_caption: Frontispiece of the first edition, engraved by Abraham Bosse, 1651

title: Discourse on Method
creator: descartes
location: Leiden, published by Jan Maire
note: Four rules of method, an autobiography of doubt, and the first appearance of 'I think, therefore I am'.
description: The Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting One's Reason and of Seeking Truth in the Sciences was published anonymously in French in Leiden in 1637 as the preface to three scientific essays, the Optics, the Meteorology and the Geometry, the last of which introduced analytic geometry. Written in French rather than Latin to reach a broad audience, it tells how Descartes, dissatisfied with his schooling, resolved to doubt everything and rebuild knowledge using four rules: accept only what is clear and distinct, divide problems, proceed from simple to complex, and review everything. Part IV gives the argument 'I think, therefore I am' and proofs of God; Part V sketches his physiology and argues that animals are machines. It is the classic manifesto of modern rationalism.
image_caption: Discourse on Method: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Meditations on First Philosophy
creator: descartes
type: Philosophical meditations (6), with objections and replies
location: Paris, published by Michel Soly
note: Radical doubt, the cogito, God as guarantor of clear ideas, and the real distinction of mind and body.
description: The Meditations on First Philosophy were published in Latin in Paris in 1641, with six sets of objections from Hobbes, Gassendi, Arnauld, Mersenne and others and Descartes' replies; a second edition followed in Amsterdam in 1642 and a French translation in 1647. In six meditations, imagined as six days, the meditator doubts the senses, the existence of the body and even mathematics, supposing an evil demon deceives him; finds that he cannot doubt that he exists while thinking; proves that God exists and is no deceiver; explains error by the will outrunning the intellect; and finally argues that mind and body are really distinct and that material things exist. Its arguments and the problems they raise, including the 'Cartesian circle' and mind-body interaction, have been at the centre of philosophy ever since.
image_caption: Meditations on First Philosophy: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Pensées
creator: pascal
type: Fragments for an apology of Christianity
location: Paris; first edition by Port-Royal, 1670
note: Notes on human wretchedness and greatness, diversion, the hidden God and the Wager.
description: At his death in 1662 Pascal left about a thousand fragments, on slips of paper later pasted into albums, for a planned defence of Christianity. His Port-Royal friends published a selection in 1670, and modern editors have argued over their intended order ever since. The fragments portray the human condition as a mix of wretchedness and greatness: we are a 'thinking reed', lost between the infinitely large and the infinitely small, and seek diversion to avoid thinking about death. Reason alone cannot reach God, who is hidden, and the heart knows truths reason cannot. The Wager argues that faced with uncertainty one should stake one's life on God, since the possible gain is infinite. The Pensées are a classic of French prose and a forerunner of existentialism.
image_caption: Title page of a 1670 Port-Royal edition

title: Theological-Political Treatise
creator: spinoza
location: Amsterdam, published anonymously by Jan Rieuwertsz with a false Hamburg imprint
note: The Bible read historically, prophecy as imagination, and a defence of freedom of thought.
description: Spinoza published the Tractatus Theologico-Politicus anonymously in 1670, with a false imprint naming Hamburg and a fictitious publisher, to defend 'the freedom to philosophise' in the Dutch Republic against Calvinist pressure. It argues that the Bible must be interpreted from the Bible itself, using history and philology; that the prophets had vivid imaginations rather than superior knowledge; that Moses did not write the Pentateuch; that miracles in the sense of breaches of natural law are impossible; and that scripture teaches obedience and charity, not philosophy. The later chapters ground the state in natural right and argue that a free republic must allow freedom of thought and speech. It was banned in 1674 and denounced across Europe as one of the most dangerous books ever written, but founded modern biblical criticism.
image_caption: Theological-Political Treatise: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Ethics
creator: spinoza
location: The Hague; published posthumously in Amsterdam in the Opera Posthuma
note: God or Nature as the one substance, the mind as the idea of the body, and freedom through understanding.
description: Spinoza worked on the Ethics, Demonstrated in Geometrical Order for some fifteen years, but did not dare publish it; his friends brought it out in the Opera Posthuma months after his death in 1677. Like Euclid's Elements it proceeds by definitions, axioms, propositions and demonstrations, with explanatory scholia. Part I argues that there is only one substance, God or Nature, and that everything follows from its nature with necessity. Part II treats the mind as the idea of the body. Parts III and IV analyse the emotions as natural phenomena and human bondage to them, and Part V shows how understanding brings freedom and the intellectual love of God. It is among the most systematic and challenging works of philosophy, admired by Goethe, Hegel, Einstein and Deleuze.
image_caption: Ethics: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding
creator: locke
location: London, printed for Thomas Basset
note: No innate ideas; all ideas come from sensation and reflection; the limits of human knowledge.
description: Locke's Essay grew from a discussion with friends around 1671 that convinced him that before investigating morality and religion they must examine the extent of human understanding. Published in December 1689 with 1690 on the title page, it went through four editions in his lifetime. Book I attacks innate ideas and principles. Book II traces all ideas to experience, sensation of the outer world and reflection on our own minds, and analyses simple and complex ideas, primary and secondary qualities, power, substance and, in a chapter added in 1694, personal identity as continuity of consciousness. Book III concerns language and Book IV knowledge, which is narrow, and probability, which must guide most of life. It founded British empiricism and dominated eighteenth-century philosophy.
image_caption: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Two Treatises of Government
creator: locke
location: London, published anonymously by Awnsham Churchill
note: Natural rights to life, liberty and property; government by consent; the right of resistance.
description: Locke published the Two Treatises anonymously in 1689, presenting them as a justification of the Glorious Revolution, though most scholars now think they were largely written around 1679–83 during the Exclusion Crisis. The First Treatise refutes Sir Robert Filmer's Patriarcha, which derived royal authority from Adam. The Second Treatise describes a state of nature governed by a law of nature, in which individuals have rights to life, liberty and property; property arises when people mix their labour with what nature provides. People consent to form political society to protect these rights more securely, and government holds power on trust: when it acts against the people's interests, they may resist and replace it. Locke acknowledged authorship only in his will. The book shaped the American Declaration of Independence and liberal constitutionalism.
image_caption: Two Treatises of Government: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: A Letter Concerning Toleration
creator: locke
location: Written in the Netherlands; published in Gouda (Latin) and London (English), 1689
note: The state cares for civil interests, the church for souls: belief cannot be compelled.
description: Locke wrote the Epistola de Tolerantia in Latin in 1685, during his Dutch exile, addressed to his friend the Remonstrant theologian Philipp van Limborch. It was published in Gouda in 1689, and an English translation by William Popple appeared the same year. Locke argues that the magistrate's authority extends only to civil interests, life, liberty, health and possessions, while care of souls belongs to each individual and voluntary churches; force cannot produce genuine belief, so persecution is both wrong and futile. His toleration had limits: he excluded Catholics, whom he regarded as owing allegiance to a foreign power, and atheists, whose oaths he thought could not be trusted. It remains a classic argument for religious liberty.
image_caption: A Letter Concerning Toleration: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Monadology
creator: leibniz
location: Vienna; first printed in German translation, Jena, 1720
note: Reality as simple soul-like substances, each mirroring the universe, in pre-established harmony.
description: Leibniz wrote this short summary of his metaphysics in French in 1714 while staying in Vienna, probably for Prince Eugene of Savoy; it had no title, and the name 'Monadology' comes from a German translation published in 1720. In ninety numbered paragraphs it describes monads, simple substances without parts, which have no windows through which anything could enter or leave; each is a living mirror of the whole universe from its own point of view, and changes only through its own internal principle. Monads differ in the clarity of their perceptions, from bare monads to souls and minds. God has pre-established a harmony among them, and among all possible worlds has chosen the best. It is the most compact statement of Leibniz's system.
image_caption: Page from Leibniz's manuscript of the Monadology

title: Theodicy
creator: leibniz
location: Amsterdam, published by Isaac Troyel
note: Why a good God permits evil: this is the best of all possible worlds.
description: The Essays of Theodicy on the Goodness of God, the Freedom of Man and the Origin of Evil, written in French and published in Amsterdam in 1710, was the only philosophical book Leibniz published in his lifetime. It grew from conversations with Queen Sophie Charlotte of Prussia and replies to the sceptic Pierre Bayle, who had argued that reason cannot reconcile evil with a good God. Leibniz coined the word theodicy, the justification of God, and argued that God, being perfectly wise, good and powerful, chose to create the best of all possible worlds; evils are permitted because they are bound up with greater goods. He distinguished metaphysical, physical and moral evil and defended human freedom. Voltaire satirised its optimism in Candide (1759).

title: New Science
creator: vico
location: Naples, published by Felice Mosca
note: The civil world was made by humans and so can be known: ages of gods, heroes and men.
description: Vico published the first New Science in Naples in 1725 and recast it completely in 1730 and again in 1744, the year of his death; the final edition opens with an allegorical frontispiece explained at length in the text, showing Metaphysic as a woman on a globe receiving a ray of light from God's eye. Vico argues that since humans made the civil world, its principles can be found in the modifications of our own mind. He traces a common course of nations through an age of gods, an age of heroes and an age of men, each with its own customs, law and language, followed by decline and recurrence. He interprets myth and Homer as the 'poetic wisdom' of early peoples. Neglected for decades, the work was revived by Michelet, Croce and Isaiah Berlin.
image_caption: New Science: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge
creator: berkeley
location: Dublin, printed by Aaron Rhames for Jeremy Pepyat
note: There is no matter: to be is to be perceived, and things exist as ideas in minds and in God.
description: Berkeley published the Principles of Human Knowledge in Dublin in 1710, at the age of twenty-five, as Part I of a larger project that he never completed. Its introduction attacks Locke's doctrine of abstract general ideas. The main text argues that the objects of human knowledge are ideas, and that the existence of a sensible thing consists in its being perceived (esse est percipi); the notion of an unperceived material substance is unintelligible. Only minds, which perceive, and their ideas exist; the order and regularity of our sensations comes from God, who also perceives things when we do not. Berkeley presented immaterialism as a defence of common sense and religion against scepticism and atheism. It was poorly received, so he restated it more accessibly in the Three Dialogues (1713).
image_caption: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous
creator: berkeley
location: London, printed by G. James for Henry Clements
note: Philonous persuades the materialist Hylas that the sensible world exists only in perception.
description: Berkeley wrote the Three Dialogues in London to make the immaterialism of the Principles more persuasive. Hylas, whose name comes from the Greek for matter, begins by defending the existence of material substance; Philonous, 'lover of mind', leads him through arguments that heat, colour, taste, shape and motion are all relative to perceivers and exist only in the mind, so that the idea of matter outside the mind is empty. By the end Hylas accepts that immaterialism is compatible with common sense, science and religion, and that things persist when unperceived because God perceives them. The dialogues are a model of clear philosophical writing and the usual introduction to Berkeley.

title: The Spirit of the Laws
creator: montesquieu
location: Geneva, published anonymously by Barrillot & Fils
note: Laws relative to climate, commerce and custom; liberty secured by separating legislative, executive and judicial powers.
description: Montesquieu spent about twenty years on De l'esprit des lois, published anonymously in Geneva in 1748. It examines laws not as abstract commands but in their relations to the form of government, climate, soil, commerce, religion, customs and population of each people. Governments are republics, animated by virtue; monarchies, animated by honour; and despotisms, animated by fear. Book XI, describing the English constitution, argues that political liberty requires that legislative, executive and judicial power be held by different bodies so that power checks power. The work criticises slavery, judicial torture and religious persecution. It was placed on the Catholic Index in 1751, went through many editions, and was a major influence on the framers of the United States Constitution.
image_file: Montesquieu, De l'Esprit des loix (1st ed, 1748, vol 1, title page).jpg
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of The Spirit of the Laws

title: Foundations of Physics (Institutions de physique)
creator: du-chatelet
location: Paris, published by Prault fils
note: Leibnizian metaphysical foundations for Newtonian physics, and a defence of vis viva.
description: Émilie du Châtelet wrote the Institutions de physique, initially as a textbook for her son, at Cirey, and published it anonymously in Paris in 1740, with a revised edition in 1742. The first chapters set out metaphysical principles for natural science, drawing on Leibniz and Christian Wolff: the principles of contradiction and sufficient reason, the nature of space, time and God. Later chapters treat matter, motion, gravity and Newtonian mechanics. She defended a role for hypotheses in science, against strict Newtonians, and argued for Leibniz's measure of force, vis viva, proportional to mass times velocity squared, which embroiled her in a public dispute with the secretary of the Academy of Sciences, Dortous de Mairan. Translated into German and Italian, the book shaped the reception of Newton and Leibniz in Europe.

title: Principia, French translation and commentary
creator: du-chatelet
location: Cirey and Lunéville; published in Paris
note: The standard French version of Newton's Principia, with an algebraic commentary.
description: In the last years of her life Du Châtelet translated Newton's Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica from Latin into French, adding a commentary that restated key parts of its geometrical arguments in the newer language of Leibnizian calculus and incorporated later work by Clairaut and others. She worked feverishly to finish it during her final pregnancy and deposited the manuscript at the Royal Library shortly before her death in 1749. It was published in 1756 and in full in 1759, with a preface by Voltaire. It remains the only complete French translation of the Principia and was the main route by which French scientists read Newton.

title: A Treatise of Human Nature
creator: hume
location: Written in La Flèche, France; published in London by John Noon and Thomas Longman
note: An attempt to introduce the experimental method into moral subjects: ideas, causation, the self, passions and morals.
description: Hume wrote the Treatise in his twenties, mostly at La Flèche in Anjou, and published it anonymously in three books: Of the Understanding and Of the Passions in 1739, Of Morals in 1740. Its subtitle calls it an attempt to introduce the experimental method of reasoning into moral subjects. It traces all ideas to impressions, argues that causal inference rests not on reason but on custom, finds that the self is nothing but a bundle of perceptions, and closes Book I in a mood of sceptical despair relieved only by backgammon and friends. Book II argues that reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and Book III that moral distinctions derive from sentiment, with the famous passage on deriving 'ought' from 'is'. Hume said it fell dead-born from the press, but it is now regarded as one of the greatest works of philosophy in English.
image_file: A Treatise of Human Nature by David Hume.jpg
image_caption: A Treatise of Human Nature: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
creator: hume
location: London, published by Andrew Millar (as Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding)
note: Hume's recast theory of knowledge: relations of ideas and matters of fact, causation, miracles.
description: Disappointed by the Treatise's reception, Hume rewrote its first book in a shorter, more elegant form, published in 1748 as Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding and retitled An Enquiry in 1758. It distinguishes relations of ideas, known by reason, from matters of fact, known by experience, and argues that our inferences from cause to effect rest on custom: we never observe necessary connection, only constant conjunction. It adds sections not in the Treatise: 'Of Miracles', which argues that no testimony can establish a miracle as the basis of religion, and an imagined speech by Epicurus against the design argument. It ends by recommending that books of school metaphysics be committed to the flames. This is the work Kant credited with waking him from his dogmatic slumber.

title: Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion
creator: hume
location: Edinburgh; published posthumously in London
note: Philo, Cleanthes and Demea debate the argument from design; Philo takes it apart.
description: Hume worked on the Dialogues for over twenty-five years and arranged for their publication after his death; they appeared in 1779, edited by his nephew. Three characters discuss what can be known of God by reason: Cleanthes defends the argument from design, comparing the world to a machine; Demea defends a priori proofs and God's incomprehensibility; and the sceptic Philo argues that the analogy is weak, that the world might as well resemble an animal or vegetable, that a designer might be imperfect or many, and that the evils of the world tell against a good and powerful creator. Which character speaks for Hume is debated, though most readers see him in Philo. The Dialogues are regarded as the most important critique of natural theology before Kant.
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion

title: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality
creator: jean-jacques-rousseau
location: Amsterdam, published by Marc-Michel Rey
note: Natural humans were free, equal and good; property and society produced inequality and dependence.
description: Rousseau wrote the Discourse on the Origin and Foundations of Inequality among Men for a prize competition of the Academy of Dijon in 1753; it did not win. He imagines humans in a pure state of nature as solitary, healthy and peaceful, moved by self-preservation and pity, and argues that philosophers such as Hobbes had projected social vices back into nature. Through the development of language, families, agriculture and metallurgy, humans became dependent on one another, and the first person who fenced off land and said 'this is mine' founded civil society and its miseries. Amour-propre, the desire for others' esteem, breeds competition and inequality, which a fraudulent social contract then entrenches as law. Voltaire mocked it, but it shaped later social criticism, including Marx.
image_caption: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: The Social Contract
creator: jean-jacques-rousseau
location: Amsterdam, published by Marc-Michel Rey
note: Man is born free and everywhere in chains: a legitimate state is one where citizens obey the general will they make.
description: Du contrat social, published in Amsterdam in 1762, asks what can make political authority legitimate. Force cannot, nor can nature; only a convention in which each person gives himself wholly to the community, so that, obeying the general will, each obeys only himself and remains free. The general will aims at the common good and differs from the 'will of all', the sum of private interests; whoever refuses to obey it will be 'forced to be free'. Sovereignty belongs to the people and cannot be represented, though government may be delegated. The work also discusses the legislator and a 'civil religion'. Banned in France and Geneva on publication, it became a bible of the French Revolution and remains one of the most debated works of political philosophy.
image_caption: The Social Contract: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Emile, or On Education
creator: jean-jacques-rousseau
type: Treatise in the form of a novel (5 books)
location: Printed in Paris under a Hague imprint, published by Jean Néaulme
note: An education according to nature, from infancy to marriage, with the 'Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar'.
description: Emile follows an imaginary pupil from birth to adulthood under a tutor who protects him from society's corruption and lets him learn from things rather than books, at the pace of his natural development. Book IV contains the 'Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar', a natural religion of conscience without revelation, which led the Paris Parlement to condemn the book and order Rousseau's arrest; it was burned in Paris and Geneva. Book V describes the education of Sophie, Emile's future wife, for a role subordinate to men, which Mary Wollstonecraft attacked. Emile transformed ideas of childhood and influenced Pestalozzi, Froebel and modern progressive education; Kant is said to have missed his daily walk while reading it.
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of Emile, or On Education

title: Encyclopédie
creator: diderot
type: Encyclopaedia (28 volumes: 17 of text, 11 of plates)
location: Paris, published by Le Breton, Briasson, David and Durand
note: The Enlightenment's 'reasoned dictionary of the sciences, arts and crafts', edited by Diderot and d'Alembert.
description: The Encyclopédie began as a project to translate Ephraim Chambers' English Cyclopaedia and became, under Diderot and at first Jean le Rond d'Alembert, the great collective work of the French Enlightenment. Its first volume appeared in 1751 with d'Alembert's Preliminary Discourse; the privilege was revoked in 1759 and the remaining ten volumes of text were printed secretly and issued together in 1765, followed by eleven volumes of plates by 1772. Its 72,000 articles, by Voltaire, Rousseau, Montesquieu, the Chevalier de Jaucourt and many others, treated the mechanical arts with the same seriousness as theology, and its cross-references were used to slip criticism past censors. Diderot discovered in 1764 that the publisher Le Breton had secretly censored the final volumes. Its frontispiece, designed by Charles-Nicolas Cochin, shows Truth unveiled by Reason and Philosophy.
image_file: Encyclopedie de D'Alembert et Diderot - Premiere Page - ENC 1-NA5.jpg
image_caption: Encyclopédie: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Rameau's Nephew
creator: diderot
location: Paris; first published in Goethe's German translation, Leipzig, 1805
note: A philosopher and a brilliant, shameless parasite debate morality, music and genius at a Paris café.
description: Diderot worked on Le Neveu de Rameau over many years and never published it. A manuscript copy reached Germany, and the first edition was Goethe's German translation of 1805; the French original appeared only in the nineteenth century, and Diderot's autograph manuscript was found in a Paris bookstall in 1890. In a café near the Palais-Royal, 'Me', a philosopher, talks with 'Him', the impoverished nephew of the composer Jean-Philippe Rameau, a cynical sponger who mimes whole operas and argues that in a corrupt society hypocrisy and flattery are the only rational strategies. The dialogue never resolves the clash between conventional morality and the nephew's exuberant amoralism. Hegel used it in the Phenomenology of Spirit as an image of the 'disrupted consciousness' of culture.

title: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
creator: adam-smith
location: London and Edinburgh, published by Andrew Millar, A. Kincaid and J. Bell
note: Morality grounded in sympathy and the judgment of an impartial spectator within the breast.
description: The Theory of Moral Sentiments grew out of Smith's lectures as professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow and made his reputation in 1759; he revised it six times, adding a substantial new part in the final edition of 1790. It opens with the observation that however selfish we may be, there are principles in our nature that interest us in others' fortunes. Sympathy, imaginatively entering into another's situation, lets us judge whether their feelings are appropriate, and we learn to judge ourselves by imagining how an impartial spectator would see us. Smith discusses propriety, merit, the role of fortune in moral judgment and the corruption of moral sentiments by admiration for the rich. The first use of 'invisible hand' in his books comes here, not in The Wealth of Nations.
image_caption: The Theory of Moral Sentiments: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: The Wealth of Nations
creator: adam-smith
location: London, published by William Strahan and Thomas Cadell
note: The division of labour, markets and the 'invisible hand', against mercantilist restrictions.
description: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, published in London in March 1776, opens with the division of labour in a pin factory, which multiplies productivity, and argues that it is limited by the extent of the market. Smith analyses prices, wages, profit and rent, the accumulation of capital and the progress of opulence, and argues that individuals pursuing their own gain are led 'as by an invisible hand' to promote the public interest. Book IV attacks the mercantile system of monopolies, tariffs and colonial restrictions; Book V discusses the duties of the state, including defence, justice, public works and education, partly to counter the stupefying effects of repetitive labour. It founded classical economics.
image_caption: The Wealth of Nations: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Critique of Pure Reason
creator: kant
location: Riga, published by Johann Friedrich Hartknoch
note: How synthetic a priori knowledge is possible, and why reason cannot know what lies beyond experience.
description: Kant published the Critique of Pure Reason in 1781 after more than a decade of near silence, and substantially revised it for the second edition of 1787; scholars cite both as A and B. It asks how synthetic judgments known a priori, such as those of mathematics and the principle that every event has a cause, are possible. The Transcendental Aesthetic argues that space and time are forms of our sensibility; the Analytic argues that the categories, such as substance and causality, are concepts of the understanding that make experience possible. The Dialectic shows that reason, trying to know the soul, the world as a whole and God beyond experience, falls into paralogisms, antinomies and failed proofs. Knowledge is thus limited to appearances, leaving room for faith and morality. It is among the most influential works of modern philosophy.

title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
creator: kant
location: Riga, published by Johann Friedrich Hartknoch
note: Good will, duty and the categorical imperative: act only on maxims you could will as universal law.
description: The Groundwork is Kant's short introduction to his moral philosophy. It begins with the claim that nothing is good without qualification except a good will, and that an action has moral worth when done from duty. The supreme principle of morality is the categorical imperative, which Kant states in several formulas: act only on a maxim you can at the same time will to be a universal law; treat humanity, in yourself and others, always as an end and never merely as a means; and act as a member of a kingdom of ends. Morality rests on the autonomy of the will, its capacity to give itself law, which presupposes freedom. Examples include false promising and suicide. It is the most widely read work of modern ethics.

title: Critique of Practical Reason
creator: kant
location: Riga, published by Johann Friedrich Hartknoch
note: The moral law as a fact of reason; freedom, God and immortality as postulates of practical reason.
description: The second Critique develops the moral philosophy of the Groundwork within the critical system. Kant argues that our consciousness of the moral law is a 'fact of reason' that reveals our freedom, which theoretical reason could not prove. The highest good, virtue crowned with proportionate happiness, requires us to postulate the immortality of the soul and the existence of God, so that practical reason achieves what theoretical reason could not. The conclusion contains the famous lines on the starry heavens above and the moral law within, which are inscribed on Kant's tomb in Königsberg.

title: Critique of Judgment
creator: kant
location: Berlin and Libau, published by Lagarde and Friederich
note: Aesthetic judgments of beauty and the sublime, and purposiveness in living nature.
description: The third Critique, the Kritik der Urteilskraft, aims to bridge the domains of nature and freedom. Its first part analyses aesthetic judgment: a judgment of beauty is disinterested, claims universal agreement without a concept, and responds to 'purposiveness without purpose' in the free play of imagination and understanding. The sublime arises when nature's vastness or power overwhelms imagination but awakens our sense of reason's superiority. Kant also discusses genius and fine art. The second part examines teleological judgment, our need to understand living organisms as if purposive. The work founded modern aesthetics and deeply influenced Schiller, the Romantics, Goethe and German idealism.
