image_caption: Title page of an early edition of Critique of Judgment

title: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
creator: wollstonecraft
location: London, published by Joseph Johnson
note: Women's apparent weakness is the product of education; reason and virtue are the same in both sexes.
description: Wollstonecraft wrote the Vindication in about six weeks and published it in January 1792, dedicating it to Talleyrand, who had proposed that girls in revolutionary France receive only domestic education. She argues that women are rational beings and that virtue, to be virtue at all, must rest on reason; women seem frivolous and dependent because they are taught from childhood to please men. She attacks Rousseau's Emile and conduct-book writers, calls for coeducation in national day schools and for women's economic independence, and hints that women should have political representation. The book was widely read and admired at first, but Godwin's frank memoir after her death turned opinion against her. It is now regarded as the founding text of liberal feminism.
image_file: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman title page.jpg
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

title: Laocoön
creator: lessing
location: Berlin, published by Christian Friedrich Voss
note: Painting and poetry have different laws: bodies in space versus actions in time.
description: Laocoön: or, On the Limits of Painting and Poetry takes its starting point from the ancient sculpture of the Trojan priest Laocoön and his sons attacked by serpents, and from the art historian Winckelmann's claim that the priest's restrained expression shows Greek nobility of soul. Lessing argues instead that the sculptor avoided the scream for reasons of the medium: visual art represents bodies coexisting in space and must choose a single pregnant moment, while poetry represents actions succeeding one another in time, so Virgil could let Laocoön cry out. He attacked the doctrine that poetry should be like painting. The book was a landmark of German aesthetics and influenced Goethe and Herder.

title: Nathan the Wise
creator: lessing
location: Berlin, published by Christian Friedrich Voss
note: A plea for toleration set in Jerusalem during the Crusades, centred on the parable of the three rings.
description: Nathan der Weise, written after the duke of Brunswick banned Lessing's theological polemics, carried his argument for toleration to the stage. In Jerusalem during the Third Crusade, the wise Jewish merchant Nathan, modelled on Moses Mendelssohn, is asked by Sultan Saladin which of the three religions is true. He answers with the parable of a father who had three identical rings made for his three sons: since the original cannot be identified, each son should prove his ring's power by love and good conduct. The play ends with the discovery that Christian, Jew and Muslim are bound by family ties. It was banned in Nazi Germany and was among the first plays staged in Berlin after the war.
image_caption: Maurycy Gottlieb, Recha welcoming her father, a scene from Nathan the Wise

title: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation
creator: bentham
location: London, published by T. Payne and Son
note: Pain and pleasure as sovereign masters; the principle of utility and the felicific calculus applied to law.
description: Bentham had the Introduction printed in 1780 as the preface to a planned penal code, but held it back and published it only in 1789. It opens by declaring that nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure, and defines the principle of utility as approving or disapproving every action by its tendency to augment or diminish the happiness of the party concerned. Bentham lists the dimensions by which pleasures and pains can be measured, intensity, duration, certainty, propinquity, fecundity, purity and extent, classifies offences and punishments, and argues that punishment is justified only when it prevents greater harm. A famous footnote asks of animals not whether they can reason or talk but whether they can suffer. It is the founding text of utilitarianism.

title: Foundations of the Entire Science of Knowledge
creator: fichte
location: Jena and Leipzig, published by Christian Ernst Gabler
note: The I posits itself and a not-I: Fichte's first full presentation of the Wissenschaftslehre.
description: Fichte published the Grundlage der gesammten Wissenschaftslehre in instalments in 1794–95 as a handbook for his students at Jena. It attempts to ground all knowledge in a single principle: the I posits itself absolutely. A second principle, the I posits a not-I, and a third, in which I and not-I mutually limit each other, generate the structures of theoretical and practical reason, deriving what Kant had simply found. The practical part presents the I as infinite striving against limitation, the root of moral life. The work was notoriously difficult; Fichte reworked the Wissenschaftslehre in many later versions. It shaped Schelling, Hegel, Hölderlin and the Romantics.

title: On Religion: Speeches to its Cultured Despisers
creator: schleiermacher
location: Berlin, published anonymously by Johann Friedrich Unger
note: Religion is neither metaphysics nor morality but a sense and taste for the infinite.
description: Schleiermacher wrote the five Speeches while a hospital chaplain in Berlin, addressing his Romantic friends who scorned religion as dogma and moralising. He argues that religion's essence is neither thinking nor acting but intuition and feeling of the universe, a 'sense and taste for the infinite', and that doctrines and institutions are secondary expressions of it. Religion appears only in particular historical forms, and he defends a community of free spirits. Published anonymously in 1799 and revised several times, the Speeches launched modern liberal Protestant theology.
image_file: Cover of 1799 edition of Über die Religion.jpg
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of On Religion: Speeches to its Cultured Despisers

title: Phenomenology of Spirit
creator: hegel
location: Bamberg and Würzburg, published by Joseph Anton Goebhardt
note: Consciousness climbs through its own contradictions, master and slave included, to absolute knowing.
description: Hegel finished the Phenomenology of Spirit in Jena in 1806, famously as Napoleon's army fought the battle outside the town, and it was published in 1807 as the first part of a planned system. It traces the 'education' of consciousness through a series of shapes, from sense-certainty, perception and understanding to self-consciousness, where the master-slave dialectic shows that self-consciousness requires recognition from another; then through reason, spirit in its historical forms from the Greek city to the French Revolution and its Terror, and religion, to absolute knowing. Each shape, examined on its own terms, collapses into contradictions that drive it to the next. Its preface attacks Schelling's absolute as 'the night in which all cows are black'. It shaped Marx, existentialism and French philosophy through Kojève's lectures.
image_caption: Phenomenology of Spirit: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Science of Logic
creator: hegel
location: Nuremberg, published by Johann Leonhard Schrag
note: The categories of thought from Being and Nothing through Essence to the Concept, developed dialectically.
description: Hegel wrote the Science of Logic while headmaster of a gymnasium in Nuremberg, publishing it in three books between 1812 and 1816; he was revising the first when he died in 1831. Logic for Hegel is not formal logic but the study of the pure categories of thought, which are also the structure of reality. It begins with pure Being, which, being wholly indeterminate, is the same as Nothing; their unity is Becoming. From there the categories of quality, quantity and measure (the Doctrine of Being), of essence, appearance and actuality (the Doctrine of Essence), and of concept, judgment, syllogism and idea (the Doctrine of the Concept) develop dialectically to the Absolute Idea. Marx and Lenin studied it closely, and it remains Hegel's most fundamental and difficult work.
image_caption: Science of Logic: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Elements of the Philosophy of Right
creator: hegel
location: Berlin, published by Nicolai
note: Freedom realised in abstract right, morality and ethical life: family, civil society and the state.
description: The Philosophy of Right appeared in Berlin in late 1820 with 1821 on the title page, which is why sources give both dates. Written as a textbook for Hegel's lectures, it describes the development of free will through abstract right (property, contract, wrong), morality (intention and conscience) and ethical life (Sittlichkeit), comprising the family, civil society, with its market economy, poverty and corporations, and the state. Its preface contains the claims that what is rational is actual and what is actual is rational, and that the owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of dusk. It was read both as an apology for the Prussian state and as a theory of modern freedom; Marx's critique of it began his own political thought.
image_caption: Elements of the Philosophy of Right: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom
creator: schelling
location: Landshut, published in Philosophische Schriften by Philipp Krüll
note: Freedom as the capacity for good and evil, rooted in a dark ground within God.
description: Schelling's essay on freedom appeared in 1809 in the first volume of his Philosophical Writings and was the last major work he published. It asks how human freedom, understood as a real capacity for good and evil, is compatible with a system in which everything is in God. Schelling distinguishes in God between existence and the ground of existence, an obscure, longing will that is in God but is not God himself; in humans, the self-will rooted in this ground can rebel against the universal will, which is the possibility of evil. Heidegger lectured on it in 1936 and called it one of the deepest works of German philosophy.

title: The World as Will and Representation
creator: schopenhauer
location: Leipzig, published by F. A. Brockhaus
note: The world as representation is appearance; its inner nature is blind will, whose striving means suffering.
description: Schopenhauer's main work appeared in December 1818 with 1819 on the title page, and was almost ignored. A second edition of 1844 added a volume of supplementary essays as long as the first, and a third edition followed in 1859. Book I presents the world as representation, structured by the principle of sufficient reason; Book II argues that the thing in itself, known from within in our own bodies, is will, a blind striving that objectifies itself in all of nature. Book III treats art as will-less contemplation of Platonic Ideas, with music as a direct copy of the will. Book IV argues that life is suffering, that compassion is the basis of morality, and that salvation lies in the denial of the will to live, comparing this to Buddhist and Hindu teaching. It deeply influenced Wagner, Nietzsche, Tolstoy, Freud and Wittgenstein.
image_caption: The World as Will and Representation: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Course of Positive Philosophy
creator: comte
location: Paris
note: The law of three stages, the hierarchy of the sciences and the founding of sociology.
description: The Cours de philosophie positive grew out of lectures Comte gave from 1826 and was published in six volumes between 1830 and 1842. It sets out the law of three stages, theological, metaphysical and positive, through which every branch of knowledge passes, and arranges the sciences in a hierarchy of increasing complexity and decreasing generality: mathematics, astronomy, physics, chemistry, biology and finally social physics, which Comte named sociology in the fourth volume (1838). Positive knowledge seeks laws relating phenomena, not hidden causes. Harriet Martineau's condensed English translation of 1853 spread positivism in Britain, where John Stuart Mill championed it.
image_file: Comte, 'Cours de philosophie positive' Wellcome L0016061.jpg
image_caption: Title page of the Cours de philosophie positive (Wellcome Collection)

title: Nature
creator: emerson
location: Boston, published anonymously by James Munroe and Company
note: The manifesto of Transcendentalism: nature as symbol of spirit, and a call to an original relation to the universe.
description: Emerson's first book was published anonymously in Boston in 1836. It opens by asking why we should not also enjoy an original relation to the universe, instead of a religion and philosophy handed down by tradition. In eight short chapters Emerson considers nature as commodity, beauty, language, discipline, idealism and spirit, arguing that natural facts are symbols of spiritual facts and that in solitude in the woods one becomes 'a transparent eye-ball' through which the currents of the Universal Being circulate. It became the manifesto of the Transcendentalist Club, founded that year, and influenced Thoreau and Whitman.

title: Essays: First Series (including 'Self-Reliance')
creator: emerson
location: Boston, published by James Munroe and Company
note: Trust thyself: 'Self-Reliance', 'The Over-Soul', 'Compensation' and other essays.
description: Emerson's first collection of essays, drawn from his lectures and journals, includes 'History', 'Self-Reliance', 'Compensation', 'Love', 'Friendship', 'Prudence', 'Heroism', 'The Over-Soul', 'Circles', 'Intellect' and 'Art'. 'Self-Reliance' urges readers to trust their own intuitions against conformity and tradition, declaring that a foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds; 'The Over-Soul' describes the universal mind in which each individual participates. The aphoristic style and the call to independence made the book one of the defining texts of American culture.

title: Walden
creator: thoreau
location: Boston, published by Ticknor and Fields
note: Two years in a cabin at Walden Pond: simplicity, attention to nature and a critique of quiet desperation.
description: Walden; or, Life in the Woods condenses into one year the two years and two months Thoreau spent, from 1845 to 1847, in a cabin he built near Walden Pond outside Concord. He wrote it over seven drafts. The book opens with 'Economy', an account of his costs and an attack on the way most men lead lives of quiet desperation, working to acquire what they do not need. Chapters on reading, sounds, solitude, visitors, the bean-field, the pond in winter and spring follow the seasons and record close observation of nature, ending with the ice breaking up and a call to awaken. It sold slowly at first but became a classic of American literature and environmental thought.
image_caption: Walden: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Resistance to Civil Government ('Civil Disobedience')
creator: thoreau
location: Boston, published in Elizabeth Peabody's Aesthetic Papers
note: Individuals must not lend themselves to the wrong they condemn; an unjust law should be openly refused.
description: Thoreau gave the lecture that became this essay after spending a night in Concord jail in July 1846 for refusing to pay his poll tax, in protest against slavery and the Mexican-American War. It was published in 1849 in Aesthetic Papers and retitled 'Civil Disobedience' after his death. He argues that conscience, not majority rule, must decide right and wrong, that a government sustaining slavery has no claim on a just man's allegiance, and that under a government which imprisons any unjustly, the true place for a just man is also a prison. Tolstoy, Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. all acknowledged its influence.

title: Democracy in America
creator: tocqueville
location: Paris, published by Charles Gosselin
note: How equality of conditions shapes laws, mores and souls, and the danger of soft despotism.
description: Tocqueville wrote Democracy in America after travelling through the United States for nine months in 1831–32. The first volume (1835) describes American institutions: the township, federalism, the judiciary and the press, and warns of the tyranny of the majority. The second volume (1840) is more philosophical, examining how equality shapes thought, feeling and habits: individualism, the love of material well-being, the art of association and the role of religion. It ends with the fear that democratic peoples may submit to an immense, tutelary power that keeps them in perpetual childhood, a soft despotism. It also includes a powerful discussion of slavery and the fate of Native Americans. It remains the most quoted book about American democracy.
image_file: Democracy in America by Alexis de Tocqueville title page.jpg
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of Democracy in America

title: A System of Logic
creator: john-stuart-mill
location: London, published by John W. Parker
note: An empiricist account of inference, with Mill's methods for finding causes and a logic of the social sciences.
description: Mill's System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive, was his first major book and established his reputation. It treats names and propositions, argues that all inference is ultimately from particulars to particulars, and that even mathematical truths are generalisations from experience. Book III sets out the five methods of experimental inquiry, agreement, difference, the joint method, residues and concomitant variations, for identifying causes. Book VI, on the logic of the moral sciences, argues for a science of human nature and society. It was a standard textbook in British universities for decades.
image_caption: A System of Logic: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: On Liberty
creator: john-stuart-mill
location: London, published by John W. Parker and Son
note: The harm principle, freedom of thought and discussion, and individuality as an element of well-being.
description: Mill published On Liberty in 1859, shortly after the death of Harriet Taylor Mill, to whom he dedicated it as joint author. It argues that the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over any member of a civilised community, against their will, is to prevent harm to others; a person's own good is not sufficient warrant. Chapter II defends freedom of thought and discussion, since a silenced opinion may be true, may contain part of the truth, and even if false keeps the truth from becoming dead dogma. Chapter III defends individuality and 'experiments of living' against the tyranny of custom and public opinion. The essay remains the classic statement of liberal individualism.
image_file: On Liberty (first edition title page via facsimile).jpg
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of On Liberty

title: Utilitarianism
creator: john-stuart-mill
location: Fraser's Magazine, London (book edition 1863)
note: Higher and lower pleasures, a proof of the principle of utility, and justice as social utility.
description: Utilitarianism appeared in three instalments in Fraser's Magazine in 1861 and as a book in 1863. Mill defends the greatest happiness principle against misunderstandings, arguing that some pleasures are higher in quality than others, so that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied, better Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied. He offers a much-criticised 'proof' that happiness is desirable because people desire it, and argues that justice is the name for the most important class of social utilities. It remains the most widely read statement of utilitarian ethics.
image_caption: Utilitarianism: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: The Subjection of Women
creator: john-stuart-mill
location: London, published by Longmans, Green, Reader and Dyer
note: The legal subordination of women is wrong in itself and a chief hindrance to human improvement.
description: Mill wrote The Subjection of Women in 1861, drawing on ideas developed with Harriet Taylor Mill and her daughter Helen Taylor, and published it in 1869 after his parliamentary campaign for women's suffrage. He argues that the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong in itself and should be replaced by perfect equality; that nothing can be known about women's 'nature' while it is distorted by subjection; and that marriage law, which made wives virtually the property of their husbands, resembles slavery. Opening professions and public life to women would double the talent available to humanity. It was widely translated and became a key text of the women's movement.
image_caption: The Subjection of Women: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: The Enfranchisement of Women
creator: harriet-taylor-mill
location: Westminster and Foreign Quarterly Review, London
note: A demand for women's equal political rights, education and employment, inspired by the Worcester convention.
description: Harriet Taylor Mill's essay was prompted by reports of the first National Woman's Rights Convention, held at Worcester, Massachusetts, in 1850. Published anonymously in the Westminster Review in July 1851 and long attributed to John Stuart Mill, it argues that women should have full equality in education, employment, property and political rights, including the vote and the right to sit in Parliament. It rejects the idea of separate spheres for the sexes, contends that women should not be confined to motherhood and domestic life, and argues that economic independence would make marriage a partnership of equals. Mill later stated that she was its author.

title: Either/Or
creator: kierkegaard
location: Copenhagen, published by C. A. Reitzel; edited by 'Victor Eremita'
note: The papers of an aesthete and of an ethical judge, posing a choice between two ways of life.
description: Either/Or, Kierkegaard's first major book, presents itself as papers found in an old writing desk by the pseudonymous editor Victor Eremita. Volume one contains the writings of 'A', a young aesthete: aphorisms, essays on Mozart's Don Giovanni and tragedy, an essay on boredom called 'The Rotation of Crops', and the 'Seducer's Diary'. Volume two contains two long letters from Judge William urging A to choose himself and take up the ethical life of marriage and vocation. The book offers no verdict, leaving the reader to choose. It was a sensation in Copenhagen and introduced Kierkegaard's theory of the stages of existence.

title: Fear and Trembling
creator: kierkegaard
location: Copenhagen, published by C. A. Reitzel; under the pseudonym Johannes de silentio
note: Abraham and Isaac: faith as a teleological suspension of the ethical that cannot be explained.
description: Published under the pseudonym Johannes de silentio on the same day as Repetition, Fear and Trembling meditates on God's command to Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. The author admires Abraham but cannot understand him: if ethics is the universal, Abraham is either a murderer or a 'knight of faith' whose relation to God stands above the ethical, a teleological suspension of the ethical. Three 'problemata' ask whether there is such a suspension, whether there is an absolute duty to God, and whether Abraham was right to keep silent. The book attacks the Hegelian claim to have gone 'further' than faith. It is often read in relation to Kierkegaard's broken engagement to Regine Olsen.
image_caption: Fear and Trembling: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: The Essence of Christianity
creator: feuerbach
location: Leipzig, published by Otto Wigand
note: Theology is anthropology: God is the projection of humanity's own essence.
description: Das Wesen des Christentums argues that religion is humanity's consciousness of its own infinite species-nature, projected outward onto an imaginary being. The attributes of God, love, wisdom, justice, are human qualities alienated from human beings, so that the more God is enriched, the poorer humanity becomes. The book examines Christian doctrines, the Trinity, incarnation, sacraments, as expressions of human needs. Its task is to bring theology back to anthropology. Engels recalled its liberating effect on the Young Hegelians, and Marx built on and criticised it. George Eliot's English translation appeared in 1854.
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of The Essence of Christianity

title: The Ego and Its Own
creator: stirner
location: Leipzig, published by Otto Wigand
note: Every ideal set above the individual is a spook; only the unique, self-owning individual is real.
description: Der Einzige und sein Eigentum, 'the unique one and his property', appeared in late 1844. Stirner argues that the Young Hegelians, in overthrowing God, have set up new sacred abstractions, Man, humanity, the state, society, morality, freedom, to which the individual is again subordinated. These are 'spooks'. The only reality is the unique individual, who owns himself and whatever he has the power to take, and who can associate with others in a voluntary 'union of egoists' rather than a state. It was briefly banned and then released as too absurd to be dangerous. Marx and Engels attacked it at length in The German Ideology.
image_caption: The Ego and Its Own: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: The Communist Manifesto
creator: marx
location: London, printed for the Communist League by J. E. Burghard
note: All history is the history of class struggles; the proletariat will overthrow the bourgeoisie.
description: Marx and Engels wrote the Manifesto of the Communist Party for the Communist League, and it was published in German in London in February 1848, just as revolutions broke out across Europe. It opens with the spectre of communism haunting Europe and declares that the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. It praises the bourgeoisie for revolutionising production and sweeping away feudal ties, but argues that capitalism creates its own gravediggers in the proletariat. It sets out the aims of communists, criticises rival socialisms, and ends with the call for workers of all countries to unite. Little noticed at first, it became one of the most widely read political documents in history.
image_caption: The Communist Manifesto: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844
creator: marx
location: Paris; first published in full in Berlin, 1932
note: Alienated labour: workers estranged from their product, their activity, their species-being and one another.
description: Marx wrote these notebooks in Paris in 1844, while studying political economy and Hegel. They were not published until 1932. The best-known section analyses alienated labour: under capitalism the worker is estranged from the product of his labour, which confronts him as an alien power; from his productive activity; from his 'species-being', the free creative activity that makes us human; and from other people. Other sections criticise Hegel's dialectic and discuss money and communism as the positive overcoming of private property. Their publication fuelled twentieth-century humanist Marxism and the debate over whether the 'young' and 'mature' Marx are one thinker.

title: Capital, Volume I
creator: marx
location: Hamburg, published by Otto Meissner
note: Commodities, surplus value and the logic of capital accumulation.
description: Das Kapital: Kritik der politischen Ökonomie, Volume I, was published in Hamburg in 1867; Volumes II and III were edited by Engels from Marx's manuscripts and published in 1885 and 1894. It begins with the commodity and its dual character as use-value and exchange-value, and the 'fetishism of commodities' that makes social relations appear as relations between things. Marx argues that labour power is a special commodity that produces more value than it costs, and that this surplus value, extracted through the working day and intensified by machinery, is the source of profit. Detailed chapters on factory legislation and 'primitive accumulation' draw on British government reports. It is the foundation of Marxist economics.
image_caption: Capital, Volume I: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint
creator: brentano
location: Leipzig, published by Duncker & Humblot
note: Intentionality as the mark of the mental, and the classification of mental phenomena.
description: Brentano's Psychologie vom empirischen Standpunkte appeared in 1874, the year he went to Vienna; only the first of a planned six books was completed, though he added material in 1911. It argues that psychology should be an empirical science based on inner perception, and that mental phenomena are distinguished from physical ones by intentional inexistence, their directedness toward an object. Mental acts are classified into presentations, judgments and phenomena of love and hate. Its doctrine of intentionality became the starting point of Husserl's phenomenology and of analytic discussions of mental content.

title: The Methods of Ethics
creator: sidgwick
location: London, published by Macmillan
note: Egoism, intuitionism and utilitarianism compared, ending in the dualism of practical reason.
description: Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics, first published in 1874 and revised through seven editions, the last after his death, examines three methods of reaching rational conclusions about what we ought to do: egoism, which aims at one's own greatest happiness; intuitionism, which relies on self-evident moral rules; and utilitarianism, which aims at the greatest happiness of all. He argues that common-sense morality is unconsciously utilitarian and that utilitarianism rests on self-evident axioms of justice, prudence and benevolence, but he cannot show that reason requires us to prefer the general good to our own when they conflict. C. D. Broad called it the best treatise on moral theory ever written.

title: How to Make Our Ideas Clear
creator: peirce
location: Popular Science Monthly, New York
note: The pragmatic maxim: our idea of anything is our idea of its sensible effects.
description: This essay, published in Popular Science Monthly in January 1878 as the second of six 'Illustrations of the Logic of Science', follows 'The Fixation of Belief'. Peirce argues that the Cartesian test of clear and distinct ideas is inadequate, and proposes a third grade of clarity: consider what effects, that might conceivably have practical bearings, we conceive the object of our conception to have; our conception of these effects is the whole of our conception of the object. Truth is the opinion fated to be ultimately agreed by all who investigate. William James later identified the essay as the birth certificate of pragmatism.

title: The Principles of Psychology
creator: william-james
location: New York, published by Henry Holt and Company
note: The stream of consciousness, habit, the self, attention and the James-Lange theory of emotion.
description: James signed a contract to write a textbook of psychology in 1878 and delivered it twelve years later, in two volumes of some 1,400 pages. It covers the brain, habit, the stream of thought, the consciousness of self, attention, memory, perception, instinct, emotion and will, mixing physiology, introspection and philosophy in vivid prose. Consciousness is described as a continuous stream rather than a chain of separate ideas, and emotion as the feeling of bodily changes that follow the perception of an exciting fact. It helped establish psychology as an independent science in America and influenced Husserl and Wittgenstein.
image_caption: The Principles of Psychology: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Pragmatism
creator: william-james
location: New York and London, published by Longmans, Green, and Co.
note: A new name for some old ways of thinking: truth as what works in the long run of experience.
description: Pragmatism: A New Name for Some Old Ways of Thinking collects eight lectures James gave at the Lowell Institute in Boston and at Columbia in 1906–07. He presents pragmatism as a method for settling metaphysical disputes, by asking what practical difference it would make if one view rather than another were true, illustrated by a squirrel circling a tree. He contrasts 'tender-minded' and 'tough-minded' temperaments, and offers pragmatism as a mediator. The sixth lecture defines true ideas as those we can assimilate, validate, corroborate and verify, a theory critics such as Russell and Moore attacked. It made pragmatism a popular philosophy.

title: Thus Spoke Zarathustra
creator: nietzsche
location: Chemnitz, published by Ernst Schmeitzner (Parts I–III); Part IV privately printed in Leipzig, 1885
note: Zarathustra preaches the Übermensch, the will to power and the eternal recurrence.
description: Nietzsche wrote Also sprach Zarathustra in short bursts between 1883 and 1885, partly in Rapallo and Sils Maria; the fourth part was printed privately in forty copies. It is a work of poetic prose in the style of scripture, in which the prophet Zarathustra descends from his mountain solitude to teach. He proclaims the Übermensch as the meaning of the earth, for which man is a rope stretched between beast and overman, and the will to power, and struggles to affirm the most abysmal thought, the eternal recurrence of all things. Nietzsche considered it his greatest book. Its imagery inspired Richard Strauss's tone poem, and its language was later exploited by nationalist readers.
image_file: Also sprach Zarathustra. Ein Buch für Alle und Keinen. In drei Theilen.jpg
image_caption: Thus Spoke Zarathustra: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Beyond Good and Evil
creator: nietzsche
location: Leipzig, published at the author's expense by C. G. Naumann
note: A prelude to a philosophy of the future: the prejudices of philosophers, master and slave morality.
description: Nietzsche published Jenseits von Gut und Böse at his own expense in 1886, subtitling it 'Prelude to a Philosophy of the Future'. It opens by asking what if truth is a woman, and attacks the prejudices of philosophers who claim to pursue truth while defending their own moral values. It discusses the will to power, the 'free spirits' of the future, religion, the natural history of morals, distinguishing master from slave morality, and the question 'what is noble?'. It restates in prose many themes of Zarathustra and leads directly to the Genealogy.
image_caption: Beyond Good and Evil: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: On the Genealogy of Morality
creator: nietzsche
location: Leipzig, published by C. G. Naumann
note: Slave morality born of ressentiment; guilt and bad conscience; the meaning of ascetic ideals.
description: Zur Genealogie der Moral was written in a few weeks in 1887 as a supplement to Beyond Good and Evil. The first essay contrasts the 'good and bad' of noble morality with the 'good and evil' of slave morality, born of the ressentiment of the weak against the strong, which Nietzsche associates with priestly Judaism and Christianity. The second traces guilt and bad conscience to debt and to instincts turned inward when humans were enclosed in society. The third asks what ascetic ideals mean and answers that humans would rather will nothingness than not will. It is the most systematic of Nietzsche's works and the model for Foucault's genealogies.
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of On the Genealogy of Morality

title: Begriffsschrift
creator: frege
location: Halle an der Saale, published by Louis Nebert
note: A 'concept-script' that introduced quantifiers and variables: the birth of modern logic.
description: Frege's Begriffsschrift, a formula language of pure thought modelled on that of arithmetic, is a slim book of under a hundred pages that created modern predicate logic. Replacing the subject-predicate analysis of traditional logic with function and argument, it introduced quantifiers that bind variables, so that statements involving 'all' and 'some', including nested ones, could be analysed precisely. It presented the first fully formal system of logic with axioms and rules of inference. Its two-dimensional notation was hard to print and read, and the book was poorly reviewed and little understood for decades. Its innovations, transmitted through Peano, Russell and Whitehead, underlie modern logic, mathematics and computer science.
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of Begriffsschrift

title: The Foundations of Arithmetic
creator: frege
location: Breslau, published by Wilhelm Koebner
note: What is a number? A non-technical case for deriving arithmetic from logic.
description: Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik, written without symbolism, criticises earlier accounts of number, psychological, empiricist (Mill's 'pebble arithmetic') and formalist, and argues that a statement of number is an assertion about a concept: 'there are four moons of Jupiter' says that the number four belongs to the concept 'moon of Jupiter'. It lays down three principles: separate the logical from the psychological, ask for the meaning of a word only in the context of a sentence, and keep concept and object distinct. Frege then defines numbers as extensions of concepts, aiming to show that arithmetic is analytic, derivable from logic. J. L. Austin's English translation of 1950 helped make it a classic of analytic philosophy.
image_file: Title page of Die Grundlagen der Arithmetik.jpg
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of The Foundations of Arithmetic

title: On Sense and Reference
creator: frege
location: Zeitschrift für Philosophie und philosophische Kritik, Leipzig
note: Why 'the morning star is the evening star' is informative: sense as mode of presentation.
description: In 'Über Sinn und Bedeutung', Frege asks how identity statements such as 'the morning star is the evening star' can be informative when 'the morning star is the morning star' is trivial. His answer is that expressions have both a reference (Bedeutung), the object they stand for, here the planet Venus, and a sense (Sinn), the mode of presentation of that object. The same distinction applies to sentences, whose reference is a truth-value and whose sense is a thought. He also discusses names without reference and indirect contexts such as belief reports. It is the founding text of the modern philosophy of language.

title: Democracy and Education
creator: dewey
location: New York, published by Macmillan
note: Education as growth through experience, and democracy as a mode of associated living.
description: Democracy and Education: An Introduction to the Philosophy of Education was Dewey's most systematic statement of his educational thought. Education is the means by which societies renew themselves, and its aim is growth, the continuous reconstruction of experience, with no end beyond more growth. Learning should be active, connected with occupations and problems, rather than passive absorption of facts, and schools should be miniature communities. Democracy is more than a form of government; it is a mode of associated living in which interests are shared and freely communicated. The book shaped progressive education worldwide.
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of Democracy and Education

title: Logical Investigations
creator: husserl
location: Halle an der Saale, published by Max Niemeyer
note: A refutation of psychologism followed by six investigations that founded phenomenology.
description: Husserl's Logische Untersuchungen appeared in two volumes in 1900 and 1901. The first, the Prolegomena to Pure Logic, attacks psychologism, the view that the laws of logic are laws of human psychology, arguing that logical truths are ideal and objective. The second contains six investigations into expression and meaning, universals, parts and wholes, grammar, intentional experiences and knowledge, describing how consciousness intends objects and how meaning is fulfilled in intuition. Husserl later called it his breakthrough work. It attracted the circle of phenomenologists in Göttingen and Munich and was decisive for the young Heidegger.

title: Creative Evolution
creator: bergson
location: Paris, published by Félix Alcan
note: Evolution driven by a creative élan vital; intellect versus intuition.
description: In L'Évolution créatrice Bergson argued that neither mechanism nor finalism can explain evolution: life is a creative current, an élan vital, that divides into diverging lines, such as plants and animals, instinct and intelligence. The intellect, evolved for acting on solid bodies, thinks in static, spatial terms and so cannot grasp life and duration; intuition, instinct become self-conscious, can. The book criticises the 'cinematographic' method of thought that reconstructs movement from snapshots. It made Bergson an international celebrity, was placed on the Catholic Index in 1914 with his other works, and influenced writers and artists from Proust to the Cubists.
image_caption: Creative Evolution: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: Principia Mathematica
creator: russell
type: Treatise in logic (3 volumes, with Alfred North Whitehead)
location: Cambridge, published by Cambridge University Press
note: An attempt to derive mathematics from logic, using the theory of types to avoid paradox.
description: Principia Mathematica, written by Whitehead and Russell over a decade, appeared in three volumes between 1910 and 1913; Cambridge University Press required the authors to contribute to the cost. It set out to show that all of pure mathematics can be derived from a small number of logical axioms and rules, carrying forward Frege's logicism while avoiding Russell's paradox with a ramified theory of types and an axiom of reducibility. It is famous for taking hundreds of pages to reach the proof that 1 + 1 = 2. Gödel's incompleteness theorems of 1931 showed that no such system can capture all mathematical truths. It nonetheless shaped modern logic, set theory and computer science.
image_caption: Principia Mathematica: early edition, manuscript or illustration

title: The Problems of Philosophy
creator: russell
location: London, Williams and Norgate (Home University Library)
note: A classic short introduction: appearance and reality, knowledge by acquaintance and the value of philosophy.
description: Russell wrote The Problems of Philosophy for the Home University Library, a popular series, calling it his 'shilling shocker'. Beginning with a table that looks different from different angles, it asks whether we can know anything about the physical world beyond sense-data, distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from knowledge by description, discusses induction, a priori knowledge, universals and truth, and closes with a chapter on the value of philosophy, which enlarges the self through contemplation of the universe even when it cannot give certain answers. It remains one of the most widely used introductions to the subject.

title: Principia Ethica
creator: g-e-moore
location: Cambridge, published by Cambridge University Press
note: 'Good' is indefinable; the naturalistic fallacy; affection and beauty as the greatest goods.
description: Principia Ethica argues that the central question of ethics, what is good, has been confused by philosophers who identify goodness with some natural property such as pleasure or what we desire. Moore calls this the naturalistic fallacy, and supports his claim with the 'open question' argument: for any proposed definition, it remains a meaningful question whether that thing is good. Goodness is a simple, non-natural property known by intuition. The final chapter names personal affection and the enjoyment of beautiful objects as by far the greatest goods. The book was adopted as a creed by the Bloomsbury Group, including Keynes and Virginia Woolf, and set the agenda for twentieth-century metaethics.
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of Principia Ethica

title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
creator: wittgenstein
location: Written largely in the Austrian army, 1914–18; published in Annalen der Naturphilosophie, Leipzig, 1921, and in London by Kegan Paul, 1922
note: The world is the totality of facts; propositions picture them; what cannot be said must be passed over in silence.
description: Wittgenstein completed the Tractatus by August 1918 and found a publisher only with Russell's help; it appeared in German in Wilhelm Ostwald's journal in 1921 and in a German-English edition with an introduction by Russell, which Wittgenstein disliked, in 1922. Its numbered remarks, from 'The world is everything that is the case' to the final 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent', argue that language pictures possible states of affairs, that logical truths are tautologies saying nothing, and that ethics, aesthetics and the meaning of life lie beyond what can be said, though they can be shown. Its own propositions are a ladder to be thrown away after climbing. It inspired the Vienna Circle, though Wittgenstein rejected their reading. The English translation is in the public domain in the United States.
image_caption: Title page of an early edition of Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus

title: Philosophical Investigations
creator: wittgenstein
location: Oxford, published by Basil Blackwell, with English translation by G. E. M. Anscombe
note: Meaning as use, language-games, family resemblance, rule-following and the private language argument.
description: Published two years after Wittgenstein's death, with Anscombe's English translation facing the German, the Investigations collects remarks he had refined since the 1930s. It opens with Augustine's picture of language learning and shows its limits through simple language-games, such as builders calling 'slab'. The meaning of a word is in most cases its use in the language; general terms like 'game' are held together by family resemblances, not shared essences. Long sections on following a rule and on sensations argue that meaning cannot be fixed by inner mental states and that a language intelligible only to its speaker is impossible. Philosophy should describe, not explain, and dissolve problems that arise when language goes on holiday. It is often ranked the most important philosophical book of the twentieth century.

title: Being and Time
creator: heidegger
location: Halle, published in the Jahrbuch für Philosophie und phänomenologische Forschung and by Max Niemeyer
note: The question of being approached through Dasein: being-in-the-world, care, anxiety and being-toward-death.
description: Sein und Zeit was published in 1927 in Husserl's yearbook, rushed into print partly to support Heidegger's candidacy for a chair, and dedicated to Husserl. It was planned in two parts of three divisions each, but only the first two divisions appeared. It aims to reawaken the question of the meaning of being by analysing Dasein, the being that we ourselves are. Dasein is being-in-the-world, encountering things first as ready-to-hand equipment; it is thrown into a world, usually absorbed in the anonymous 'they', and its being is care. Anxiety and anticipation of one's own death can call Dasein to authenticity, and its being is grounded in temporality. Its vocabulary and analyses shaped existentialism, hermeneutics and deconstruction.

title: Philosophy in a New Key
creator: langer
location: Cambridge, Massachusetts, published by Harvard University Press
note: Discursive and presentational symbols: music, myth and ritual as articulations of feeling.
description: Philosophy in a New Key: A Study in the Symbolism of Reason, Rite, and Art argued that a new 'generative idea' was transforming philosophy: the recognition that human beings are essentially symbol-makers. Langer distinguished discursive symbolism, the linear, conventional form of language, from presentational symbolism, which presents a complex meaning all at once, as in images, ritual, myth and above all music, which she held articulates the forms of feeling. The book became one of the best-selling philosophy titles of its era and led to her theory of the arts in Feeling and Form.

title: Natural Right and History
creator: leo-strauss
location: Chicago, published by the University of Chicago Press
note: Against historicism and fact-value relativism, a case for revisiting the classical idea of natural right.
description: Based on Strauss's Walgreen Lectures of 1949, Natural Right and History argues that modern social science, through historicism and Max Weber's distinction between facts and values, has abandoned the idea that reason can know what is right by nature, leading to relativism and nihilism. Strauss contrasts classic natural right, in Socrates, Plato, Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas, with modern natural right in Hobbes and Locke, and treats Rousseau and Burke as signs of the crisis. It is the most influential statement of his call to reopen the quarrel between the ancients and the moderns.

title: The Concept of Mind
creator: ryle
location: London, published by Hutchinson
note: Descartes's 'ghost in the machine' is a category mistake; knowing how is not knowing that.
description: The Concept of Mind attacks what Ryle calls the 'official doctrine', descended from Descartes, that a person is a body plus a mind, a ghost in a machine whose private episodes cause public behaviour. He argues that this rests on a category mistake, like asking where the university is after seeing all the colleges. Talk of intelligence, will, emotion, sensation and imagination is mainly about dispositions and ways of acting. Knowing how, a practical capacity, is not reducible to knowing that, a set of propositions. The book was a landmark of Oxford philosophy and of logical behaviourism.

title: Truth and Method
creator: gadamer
location: Tübingen, published by J. C. B. Mohr (Paul Siebeck)
note: Understanding as a fusion of horizons, prejudice rehabilitated, and the authority of tradition.
description: Wahrheit und Methode: Grundzüge einer philosophischen Hermeneutik argues that understanding in the humanities is not a matter of method but an event of truth. Part One uses the experience of art, which addresses us and changes us, against aesthetic detachment. Part Two develops a hermeneutics of historical understanding: prejudices, or pre-judgments, are conditions of understanding; we stand within an effective history; and understanding is a fusion of the interpreter's horizon with that of the text. Part Three makes language the medium of all understanding. It prompted a famous debate with Habermas over tradition and critique.

title: The Logic of Scientific Discovery
creator: popper
location: Vienna, published by Julius Springer (as Logik der Forschung); English edition London, Hutchinson, 1959
note: Science advances by bold conjectures and attempted refutations; falsifiability as the mark of science.
description: Popper's Logik der Forschung appeared in Vienna in 1934 in a series edited by members of the Vienna Circle, though it attacked their verificationism. He argued that induction cannot justify universal theories, but a single contrary observation can falsify one, so scientific method consists in proposing bold, testable conjectures and trying to refute them. Falsifiability, not verifiability, demarcates science from non-science. Theories survive only provisionally. The enlarged English version of 1959 made it one of the most influential works in the philosophy of science.

title: The Open Society and Its Enemies
creator: popper
location: Written in Christchurch, New Zealand; published in London by Routledge
note: Plato, Hegel and Marx as enemies of an open, self-critical society; against historicism.
description: Popper wrote The Open Society in New Zealand during the Second World War, as what he called his war effort. Volume I, The Spell of Plato, reads the Republic as a blueprint for a closed, totalitarian society; Volume II, The High Tide of Prophecy, attacks Hegel and Marx for historicism, the belief in inexorable laws of historical development. Against utopian planning he defends an open society in which institutions can be criticised and changed peacefully, and piecemeal social engineering. Classicists have disputed his reading of Plato, but the book became a classic of postwar liberalism.

title: Language, Truth and Logic
creator: vienna-circle
location: London, published by Victor Gollancz
note: A. J. Ayer's polemical English statement of logical positivism and the verification principle.
description: A. J. Ayer, aged twenty-five, wrote Language, Truth and Logic after visiting the Vienna Circle in 1933, and it became the best-known English statement of logical positivism. It argues that a sentence is literally meaningful only if it is analytic or empirically verifiable; metaphysics, theology and ethics are therefore nonsense. Moral judgments express feelings rather than state facts, a view known as emotivism. Philosophy's task is analysis, not the discovery of truths about the world. Ayer later admitted that most of the book was false, but it was widely read and debated.

title: Dialectic of Enlightenment
creator: frankfurt-school
type: Philosophical fragments (by Max Horkheimer and Theodor W. Adorno)
location: Written in Los Angeles; mimeographed in New York, 1944; published in Amsterdam by Querido, 1947
note: Enlightenment reverts to myth: instrumental reason, domination of nature and the culture industry.
description: Horkheimer and Adorno wrote Dialectik der Aufklärung in exile in California during the Second World War. They argue that Enlightenment, which aimed to free humanity from fear and myth by mastering nature, has turned into a new myth: reason has become instrumental, a tool of domination over nature and over human beings, culminating in fascism. The book reads Homer's Odysseus as a prototype of the bourgeois self, treats the Marquis de Sade as Enlightenment's dark twin, analyses the 'culture industry' that mass-produces entertainment to secure conformity, and examines antisemitism. It became a founding text of critical theory.

title: Being and Nothingness
creator: sartre
location: Paris, published by Gallimard
note: Consciousness as nothingness, radical freedom, bad faith and the look of the other.
description: L'Être et le néant: essai d'ontologie phénoménologique was published in occupied Paris in 1943. Drawing on Husserl and Heidegger, Sartre distinguishes being-in-itself, the solid being of things, from being-for-itself, consciousness, which is a nothingness, always beyond what it is. Human beings are condemned to be free and wholly responsible, and bad faith is self-deception about that freedom, illustrated by the café waiter and the woman on a date. In being-for-others, the look of another person makes me an object, and relations with others are marked by conflict. The book ends with existential psychoanalysis. It was the major philosophical work of French existentialism.

title: Existentialism Is a Humanism
creator: sartre
location: Delivered at the Club Maintenant, Paris, October 1945; published by Nagel, Paris, 1946
note: Existence precedes essence: in choosing for ourselves, we choose for all humanity.
description: Sartre gave this lecture to a packed crowd in Paris on 29 October 1945, and its publication made existentialism a fashion. He answers critics who called existentialism pessimistic and immoral by arguing that for human beings existence precedes essence: there is no human nature, no God to define us, and we are nothing but what we make ourselves. In choosing, we choose an image of humanity for everyone, which brings anguish, abandonment and despair, but also responsibility. His example of a student deciding whether to join the Free French or stay with his mother illustrates that no ethical theory can decide for us. Sartre later expressed regret at its popularity.

title: The Second Sex
creator: beauvoir
location: Paris, published by Gallimard
note: One is not born, but becomes, a woman: woman made the Other in biology, history, myth and lived experience.
description: Le Deuxième Sexe appeared in two volumes in 1949 and sold over twenty thousand copies in its first week; the Vatican put it on the Index. Volume I, Facts and Myths, examines what biology, psychoanalysis and historical materialism say about women, traces women's history and analyses the myths of woman in literature. Volume II, Lived Experience, opens with the claim that one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman, and follows women's formation from childhood through sexual initiation, marriage, motherhood and old age, closing with the independent woman. Throughout, Beauvoir argues that man has made himself the Subject and woman the Other. A complete English translation appeared only in 2009.

title: The Ethics of Ambiguity
creator: beauvoir
location: Paris, published by Gallimard
note: An existentialist ethics: to will oneself free is to will others free.
description: Pour une morale de l'ambiguïté answers the charge that existentialism cannot ground an ethics. Beauvoir argues that human beings are ambiguous, both free subjects and objects among others, and that ethics begins from accepting this condition rather than fleeing it. She describes attitudes of bad faith, the sub-man, the serious man, the nihilist, the adventurer and the passionate man, and argues that genuine freedom requires willing the freedom of others. The final part discusses the use of violence in political struggle. It is often recommended as the clearest statement of existentialist ethics.

title: The Origins of Totalitarianism
creator: arendt
location: New York, published by Harcourt, Brace and Company
note: Antisemitism, imperialism and totalitarianism: a new form of rule through terror and ideology.
description: Arendt's first major book, written in the late 1940s, traces the elements that 'crystallised' into Nazism and Stalinism. Part One examines modern antisemitism; Part Two examines imperialism, race-thinking and the decline of the nation-state, including the plight of stateless people who had lost 'the right to have rights'. Part Three analyses totalitarianism as a novel form of government that uses ideology and terror to dominate every aspect of life, with the concentration camp as its central institution, aiming to make human beings superfluous. A chapter on 'Ideology and Terror' was added in 1958. It established her reputation.

title: The Human Condition
creator: arendt
location: Chicago, published by the University of Chicago Press
note: Labour, work and action; politics as speech and deeds among plural equals in public.
description: The Human Condition, based on Arendt's Walgreen Lectures of 1956, distinguishes three fundamental activities: labour, which meets biological needs and leaves nothing behind; work, which fabricates a durable world of objects; and action, speech and deeds among plural equals, through which individuals disclose who they are and begin something new. The ancient Greek polis gave action a public space; modernity has elevated labour and consumption and absorbed public and private into 'the social'. The prologue reflects on Sputnik and the wish to escape the earth. It is her major work of political philosophy.

title: Eichmann in Jerusalem
creator: arendt
location: New York, published by Viking Press, after appearing in The New Yorker
note: A report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann and 'the banality of evil'.
description: Arendt attended Eichmann's trial in Jerusalem in 1961 for The New Yorker, where her report appeared in five instalments before the book. She portrayed Eichmann not as a fanatical monster but as a careerist incapable of thinking from another's standpoint, coining the subtitle 'a report on the banality of evil'. Her remarks on the role of the Jewish councils in the deportations provoked fierce controversy and broke friendships. Later historians, using sources unavailable to her, have argued that Eichmann was a more committed antisemite than she allowed, while her concept of thoughtlessness remains widely discussed.

title: Totality and Infinity
creator: levinas
location: The Hague, published by Martinus Nijhoff
note: The face of the other breaks totality and calls me to infinite responsibility; ethics as first philosophy.
description: Totalité et Infini: essai sur l'extériorité was Levinas's doctoral thesis and first major work. He argues that Western philosophy, from Plato to Heidegger, has been a philosophy of totality, reducing the other to the same. Against this, he describes the face-to-face encounter: the face of the other person expresses an infinity that exceeds any idea I can have of it, and commands 'thou shalt not kill'. Ethics, the relation to the other, precedes ontology. The book also offers phenomenologies of enjoyment, dwelling, eros and fecundity. Derrida's long essay 'Violence and Metaphysics' (1964) responded to it.

title: Phenomenology of Perception
creator: merleau-ponty
location: Paris, published by Gallimard
note: The lived body as the subject of perception; we are in the world before we reflect on it.
description: Phénoménologie de la perception argues that perception is our primary access to the world and that neither empiricism nor intellectualism can account for it. Drawing on Husserl, Gestalt psychology and neurological case studies, notably the brain-injured patient Schneider and phantom limbs, Merleau-Ponty shows that the subject of perception is the lived body, with its motor intentionality, habits and body schema, already engaged in a meaningful world. Later parts treat space, sexuality, speech, other people, the cogito, temporality and freedom. Its preface is a classic short account of phenomenology.

title: Two Dogmas of Empiricism
creator: quine
location: The Philosophical Review, Ithaca, New York
note: No sharp analytic-synthetic distinction and no statement-by-statement verification: knowledge as a web.
description: First presented to the American Philosophical Association in December 1950 and published in The Philosophical Review in 1951, this essay attacks two assumptions of logical empiricism: that there is a sharp distinction between analytic truths, true by meaning, and synthetic truths, true by fact; and reductionism, the idea that each meaningful statement can be confirmed or refuted on its own by experience. Quine argues that attempts to define analyticity go in a circle, and that our statements face experience as a corporate body, a web of belief in which any statement can be revised. It is one of the most cited philosophy papers of the twentieth century.

title: Gravity and Grace
creator: simone-weil
location: Paris, published by Plon; edited by Gustave Thibon
note: Notebook thoughts on attention, affliction, decreation and the void that grace fills.
description: La Pesanteur et la grâce is a selection from the notebooks Weil left with the Catholic farmer-philosopher Gustave Thibon in 1942, arranged by him under thematic headings and published in 1947. In short, intense entries she contrasts gravity, the natural force by which souls, like bodies, sink toward self-interest and power, with grace, which descends only into a void we leave open. She writes on attention, affliction, 'decreation' of the self, the love of God and of the world, and the beauty of necessity. Because Thibon chose and ordered the fragments, scholars recommend reading it alongside the complete notebooks.

title: Time and Narrative
creator: ricoeur
location: Paris, published by Éditions du Seuil
note: Narrative configures the lived experience of time, in history and in fiction.
description: Temps et récit sets Augustine's aporias of time against Aristotle's theory of plot, arguing that narrative is the means by which human beings make time their own. Ricoeur describes a threefold mimesis, the prefiguration of action, its configuration in a plot, and its refiguration in the reader's life, and examines how historiography and fiction each refer to time. The third volume explores the interweaving of history and fiction and leads to the idea of narrative identity, developed in Oneself as Another.

title: Intention
creator: anscombe
location: Oxford, published by Basil Blackwell
note: Intentional action as action to which a certain sense of the question 'why?' applies.
description: Intention, under a hundred pages long, is regarded as the founding work of the modern philosophy of action. Anscombe asks what distinguishes intentional actions and argues that they are those to which a certain sense of the question 'why?' is given application, where the answer gives a reason for acting. The same action may be intentional under one description and not another: a man pumping water may also be poisoning the household. Her discussion of practical knowledge, knowledge of what one is doing without observation, and of the 'direction of fit' of intentions has been central ever since.

title: Modern Moral Philosophy
creator: anscombe
location: Philosophy (journal), London
note: Moral 'ought' is a relic of a law conception without a lawgiver; return to the virtues.
description: Anscombe's article, published in the journal Philosophy in 1958, argues that moral philosophy should be set aside until we have an adequate philosophy of psychology; that the concepts of moral obligation and the specifically moral 'ought' are survivals of a divine law conception of ethics that no longer makes sense without belief in a lawgiver; and that the differences between English moral philosophers from Sidgwick onward are of little importance, since all of them accept that it might be right to do anything if the consequences are good enough. She coined the term 'consequentialism' here. The paper is widely credited with launching the modern revival of virtue ethics.

title: The Sovereignty of Good
creator: murdoch
location: London, published by Routledge and Kegan Paul
note: Moral life as attention to reality; unselfing; the Good as a real, magnetic ideal.
description: The Sovereignty of Good collects three essays: 'The Idea of Perfection', 'On "God" and "Good"' and 'The Sovereignty of Good over Other Concepts'. Murdoch argues against existentialist and analytic pictures of the moral agent as a will that chooses, and proposes instead that moral life goes on continually in what we attend to. Her example of a mother-in-law, M, who learns to see her daughter-in-law D justly shows moral progress with no outward act. The fat, relentless ego distorts vision; beauty in nature and art and intellectual disciplines can unself us. The Good is real and transcendent, like the sun in Plato. The book is short and hugely influential.

title: Beast and Man
creator: midgley
location: Ithaca, New York, published by Cornell University Press
note: Humans as animals with a nature; ethology and evolution as resources for ethics.
description: In Beast and Man: The Roots of Human Nature, Midgley argued that philosophers had ignored the fact that human beings are animals, and drew on ethology to show that we have a characteristic nature, including instincts and motives that structure our lives without determining them. She criticised both those who deny human nature altogether and crude sociobiological reductions, and argued that understanding our nature helps rather than threatens ethics. The book established her as a leading critic of scientism and a writer on animals and the environment.

title: A Theory of Justice
creator: rawls
location: Cambridge, Massachusetts, published by the Belknap Press of Harvard University Press
note: Justice as fairness: principles chosen behind a veil of ignorance, including the difference principle.
description: A Theory of Justice develops ideas Rawls had worked on since the 1950s into a systematic alternative to utilitarianism. Imagining free and equal persons in an 'original position' behind a veil of ignorance, not knowing their class, talents or conception of the good, he argues that they would choose two principles: equal basic liberties for all, and social and economic inequalities arranged so that they attach to positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity and benefit the least advantaged. The method of reflective equilibrium adjusts principles and considered judgments to each other. It revived Anglo-American political philosophy and provoked responses from Nozick, Sandel, MacIntyre, Sen and Nussbaum.

title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
creator: kuhn
location: Chicago, published by the University of Chicago Press (International Encyclopedia of Unified Science)
note: Normal science, anomaly, crisis and paradigm shift.
description: Kuhn's book first appeared as a monograph in the International Encyclopedia of Unified Science, a series founded by logical positivists. Drawing on the history of science, it argues that mature sciences work within paradigms, shared exemplars and assumptions that define the puzzles of normal science. Anomalies accumulate, provoke crisis, and are resolved by revolutions in which a new paradigm replaces the old, as when Copernican astronomy replaced Ptolemaic, and scientists afterwards work in a different world. Competing paradigms are partly incommensurable. A 1969 postscript answered critics. It is one of the most cited academic books ever written.

title: Discipline and Punish
creator: foucault
location: Paris, published by Gallimard (as Surveiller et punir)
note: From public torture to the prison: disciplinary power, surveillance and the Panopticon.
description: Surveiller et punir: naissance de la prison opens with the gruesome public execution of the would-be regicide Damiens in 1757 and contrasts it with a prison timetable of eighty years later. Foucault argues that the shift from spectacular punishment to imprisonment was not simply humane progress but the rise of a new form of power, discipline, which works through surveillance, examination and normalisation to produce docile, useful bodies, in schools, armies, factories and hospitals as well as prisons. Bentham's Panopticon is its emblem. Knowledge of individuals and power over them grow together. The book became a foundational text across the social sciences.

title: After Virtue
creator: macintyre
location: Notre Dame, Indiana, published by the University of Notre Dame Press; London, Duckworth
note: Modern morality as fragments; virtues, practices, narrative and tradition.
description: After Virtue: A Study in Moral Theory opens with a 'disquieting suggestion': that our moral language is in the state of the natural sciences after an imagined catastrophe, surviving in fragments whose original context has been lost. MacIntyre argues that the Enlightenment project of justifying morality without a conception of human purpose failed, leaving emotivism and interminable disagreement. He offers instead an Aristotelian account of virtues defined through practices, the narrative unity of a human life and living traditions, and ends by suggesting that we await a new, very different St Benedict. It transformed the debate about virtue ethics and liberalism.

title: Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy
creator: bernard-williams
location: London, published by Fontana; Cambridge, Massachusetts, Harvard University Press
note: Against the ambitions of moral theory; 'morality' as a peculiar institution.
description: Williams asks Socrates' question, how one should live, and argues that philosophy cannot answer it in the way ethical theories, Kantian or utilitarian, try to. He distinguishes thick ethical concepts like cruelty and courage from thin ones like good and right, argues that reflection can destroy ethical knowledge, and criticises 'the morality system', with its focus on obligation and blame, as a peculiar institution. He holds that ethics could be objective only in a limited way, grounded in human needs and practices. It is his most sustained book on ethics.

title: A Defense of Abortion
creator: judith-jarvis-thomson
location: Philosophy & Public Affairs, Princeton
note: Even if the foetus is a person, its right to life does not include a right to use another's body.
description: Published in the first volume of Philosophy & Public Affairs, Thomson's article grants, for the sake of argument, that the foetus is a person from conception and asks whether abortion is then always wrong. She imagines waking up with a famous unconscious violinist plugged into your kidneys, who will die if disconnected in the next nine months, and argues that you are not morally required to stay connected: a right to life does not include the right to use another person's body. She discusses rape, contraception failure and 'Good Samaritan' versus 'Minimally Decent Samaritan' duties. It is among the most reprinted articles in philosophy.

title: Of Grammatology
creator: derrida
location: Paris, published by Éditions de Minuit
note: Western metaphysics privileges speech over writing; reading Rousseau and Saussure against themselves.
description: De la grammatologie argues that Western thought has been governed by 'logocentrism', the privileging of speech as the immediate presence of meaning, with writing treated as a secondary, dangerous supplement. Reading Saussure, Lévi-Strauss and above all Rousseau's Essay on the Origin of Languages, Derrida shows how their texts depend on the writing they disparage, and develops ideas of the trace, différance and the supplement. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak's English translation of 1976, with a long preface, made it central to literary theory in the English-speaking world.

title: The Concept of Representation
creator: pitkin
location: Berkeley, published by the University of California Press
note: Authorisation, accountability, standing for and acting for: the uses of a contested concept.
description: Based on her Berkeley dissertation, Pitkin's book uses ordinary language analysis to map the uses of 'representation'. She distinguishes formalistic views, which see representation in authorisation (Hobbes) or accountability; descriptive representation, in which representatives resemble those they represent; symbolic representation; and substantive representation, acting in the interest of the represented in a manner responsive to them. She argues that the mandate-independence controversy cannot be settled as usually posed. It remains the standard starting point for research on political representation.

title: Reasons and Persons
creator: parfit
location: Oxford, published by Clarendon Press
note: Self-defeating theories, personal identity and what matters, the non-identity problem, the repugnant conclusion.
description: Reasons and Persons has four parts. The first argues that some moral and rational theories are self-defeating. The second examines our attitudes to time. The third, using thought experiments about teleportation and divided brains, argues that personal identity is not what matters: what matters is psychological connectedness and continuity, and accepting this can make us less self-concerned and less afraid of death. The fourth turns to future generations, posing the non-identity problem and the 'repugnant conclusion' of population ethics. It is one of the most influential works of moral philosophy since Sidgwick.

title: Animal Liberation
creator: peter-singer
location: New York, published by New York Review / Random House
note: Speciesism is like racism: the capacity to suffer, not species, is what counts.
description: Animal Liberation grew from Singer's 1973 review in The New York Review of Books. He argues that the principle of equal consideration of interests applies to all beings who can suffer, and that giving lesser weight to animals' interests simply because they belong to another species, speciesism, is a prejudice like racism or sexism. Detailed chapters document animal experimentation and factory farming. The book ends with practical recommendations, including vegetarianism. It became a founding text of the animal rights movement, and Singer published a substantially revised edition, Animal Liberation Now, in 2023.

title: Famine, Affluence, and Morality
creator: peter-singer
location: Philosophy & Public Affairs, Princeton
note: If we can prevent something very bad at little cost, we ought to: the drowning child and global poverty.
description: Written during the 1971 famine and refugee crisis in East Bengal, Singer's article argues that suffering and death from lack of food, shelter and medical care are bad, and that if it is in our power to prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. If I pass a child drowning in a shallow pond, I ought to wade in even at the cost of muddy clothes; distance and the number of others who could help make no moral difference. The conclusion is that the affluent should give far more than is customary, and that the line between duty and charity must be redrawn. It inspired the effective altruism movement.

title: The Fragility of Goodness
creator: nussbaum
location: Cambridge, published by Cambridge University Press
note: Luck and ethics in Greek tragedy and philosophy: the good life is vulnerable.
description: The Fragility of Goodness: Luck and Ethics in Greek Tragedy and Philosophy examines how Aeschylus, Sophocles, Euripides, Plato and Aristotle dealt with the fact that much of what matters to a good human life, friends, love, political community, health, is exposed to fortune. Nussbaum reads Plato as seeking a self-sufficient good beyond luck, and defends Aristotle, and the tragic poets, for accepting that a good life is vulnerable and that the emotions are a form of perception. The book argued that literature is a resource for moral philosophy.
